Cuckoo search is considered an evolutionary algorithm proposed by Deb and Yang in the 
year 2009 (Yang and Deb, 2009). This algorithm is termed a search strategy model on the 
cuckoo species’ family parasitism, which lay th eir eggs in other host birds’ nests. If the 
host bird identifies these eggs, it will return  and form a new nest somewhere or fling 
these alien eggs. Every cuckoo species ca n modify its position when time passes and 
focused on one new solution from every egg in the nest as shown in Figure 3. 
The worst solution is replaced by this new solution. Only the three perfect rules are 
used which are considered as: 
1 Every cuckoo lays one egg at a time and is  put up in other nests which are selected 
randomly. 
2 For next-generation, better nests with a higher quality of eggs are considered. 
3 No. of available other host nest is a fi xed and suitable host which discovers the alien 
egg with P ∈ [0, 1] probability.

Abstract: Computer-aided tools are becoming increasingly important in medical diagnostics. This paper introduces the Efficient Feature 
Extraction Bas ed Recurrent Neural Network ( FERNN) for computer -aided t hyroid disease prediction. The FERNN model uses a Gated 
Recurrent Unit Recurrent Neural Network (GRU -RNN) optimized with the COOT Optimization Algorithm.The study begins by gathering data 
from an open -source system and preprocessing it using min -max normalization to address missing values. The preprocessed data unde rgoes a 
two-level feature extraction (TLFE) procedure. In the first level, a ranked filter feature set technique is used to prioritize fe atures based on 
medical expert recommendations. In the second level, a variety of metrics, including information gain, gain ratio, chi -square, and relief, are used 
to rank and select features. A composite measure guided by fuzzy logic is then used to select a jud icious subset of features. The FERNN model 
uses the GRU -RNN to classify thyroid diseases in the databases. To op timise, the COOT optimization method is employed.  The model's 
weights. The FERNN model was put into practise in MATLAB and assessed with a  variety of statistical metrics, including kappa, accuracy, 
precision, recall, sensitivity, specificity, and the F -measure. The proposed methodology was benchmarked against traditional techniques, 
including the deep belief neural network (DBN), artificial neural network (ANN), and support vector machine (SVM). 
Keywords: Thyroid disease classification, Feature retrieval, gated recurrent unit (GRU), recurrent neural network (RNN),  Two-level feature 
extraction (TLFE), Fuzzy logic, Information gain, Gain ratio, Chi-square, Relief, Changes. 
 
1. Introduction 
The thyroid, resembling a butterfly in shape, is a 
significant gland situated in the lower neck region and pivotal 
in regulating the body's metabolism [1]. It produces two vital 
hormones, triiodothyronine (T3) and levothyroxine (T4), 
pivotal for protein synthesis, temperature control, and overall 
energy management [2]. This gland is susceptible to a range of 
often perplexing diseases, with hypothyroidism and 
hyperthyroidism being common occurrences [3]. Insufficient 
thyroid hormone secretion causes hypothyr oidism, and 
excessive thyroid hormone secretio n causes hypertension 
release. The former leads to weight gain, a swollen neck, and a 
slow heart rate, while the latter entails elevated blood pressure, 
a heightened heart rate, and weight loss [4] [5]. 
In developed nations, an estimated 4 –5% of individuals are 
affected by hypothyroidism. Its potential consequences include 
elevated cholesterol levels, hypertension, cardiovascular 
complications, stunted growth in adolescents, and depression 
[7] and [8]. Thus, educating the populace about its symptoms, 
categories, and origins is of paramount importance. Diagnosing 
thyroid disorders often involves blood tests to Check the 
concentrations of TSH, T3, and T4 [9]. The health  domain 
offers an abundance of intricat e data, posing significant 
challenges. To address this, artificial intelligence (AI) 
techniques are emerging to detect and diagnose evolving 
diseases [10].

Neural Networks, K-nearest neighbor (KNN), Artificial Neural

2. Literature Review 
In recent years, numerous advancements in deep learning 
methodologies for automatic thyroid disease detection have 
been introduced by researchers. This section offers a concise 
overview of notable research endeavors in this field. 
Tahir Alyas et al. [11] devised an empirical AI -driven 
method for predicting thyroid infections. Various AI 
techniques, including ANN, KNN, random forest algorithms, 
and decision trees, were evaluated on a dataset to enhance 
disease prediction within predefined boundaries. They 
achieved remarkable accuracy of 94.8% and specificity of 91% 
using the random forest algorithm. 
Hafiz Abbad Ur Rehman et al. [12] Developed variants of 
the K -nearest neighbours (KNN) algorithm for identifying 
thyroid disorders. KNN using L1 -based selection, KNN with 
chi-square-based choice of features, and KNN without 
choosing features  were among the variants. KEEL Dataset 
Collection: Thyroid Tumours  were used, as well as a dataset 
from a Pakistani clinic. The later dataset included three 
additional attributes: pulse rate, BMI, and blood pressure. 
Mehdi Hosseinzadeh et al. [13] developed a neural network 
for thyroid recognition called multiple multi -layer perceptron 
(MMLP). They improved the network's learning rate 
computation by resolving issues with local minima and back -
propagation error computations. The MMLP model 
demonstrated enhanced overall classification performance for 
thyroid disorders, attaining a 0.7% accuracy improvement 
when compared to a standalone system. 
Rajasekhar Chaganti et al. [14] investigated AI and deep 
learning feature design strategies. Robustness was introduced 
into their approach via additional resilience, inverted feature 
removal, forward choice of characteristics, unilateral 
component choices, and AI-based tree learners’ considerations. 
Their proposed method accurately identified thyroid disease of 
the immune system, swollen regulation protein, thyroid disease 
brought on by the condition known as Ha, and non -thyroid 
disease (NDIS), with the sel ected additive tree classifier 
outperforming others and generating an F1 score of 0.94. 
K. Shankar et al. [15] suggested a feature -based multi -
kernel SVM met hod for thyroid identification diseases. Their 
approach made use of fine component selection as well as a 
region-based classification process. Using "Multi Kernel 
Support Vector Machine," they organized data sequences and 
implemented a comprehensive feature selection method. 
Through advanced dark wolf development, the model 
attempted to improve characterization performance by raising 
the significance of non -essential variables and refining  models 
from varied datasets.

5. Conclusion 
This paper introduces the Feature Extraction B ased 
Recurrent Neural Network ( FERNN) for computer -aided 
thyroid disease prediction, highlighting the increasing 
importance of computer -aided tools in medical diagnostics. 
The paper presents a method for thyroid disease prediction 
using a Gated Recurrent Unit within Recurrent Neural 
Networks, optimized with the COOT Optimization 
Algorithm.The methodology follows a systematic sequence of 
steps, beginning with the collection of databases from open -
source platforms. A preprocessing protocol is then established 
to address missing values using the normalization method of 
min-max. The preprocessed dataset is subjected to feature 
extraction through the Two -Level Feature Extraction (TLFE) 
approach. The initial phase (Level 1) employs the method of 
ranking filter sets features , guided by expert recommendations 
and reinforced through label -driven validation. In Level 2, 
features are meticulously evaluated and selected using metrics 
like information gain, gain ratio, chi -square, and relief. 
Effective features are identified employing a combined 
indicator with a fuzzy basis.  The process concludes with the 
implementation of the GRU -RNN model for thyroid disease 
classification, fine -tuning weight selection through the COOT 
Optimization Algorithm. Performance evaluation is executed 
using MATLAB, rigorously assessing metrics such as 
sensitivity, kappa, F -measure, recall, specificity, accuracy, and 
precision. The suggested approach is thoroughly benchmarked 
against industry standard  methods, including ANN, SVM, and

abstract  
The rational design of metal ion-doped transition metal oxides has been considered as a novel electrode 
material for the development of high-performance asymmetric supercapacitors (ASCs). Herein, we facilely 
synthesized molybdenum and vanadium doped zinc oxide (Mo- and V-doped ZnO) lotus flower-like hier-
archical structures using the co-precipitation method for use as a high capacity cathode material for ASCs. 
The formation mechanism during the self-assembly growth and highly faceted Mo- and V-doped ZnO lotus 
flowers were examined. Utilizing the beneficial properties of high electrochemical conductivity and ex-
cellent electroactive area, Mo- and V-doped ZnO lotus flowers demonstrated maximum specific capacities 
of 336 C g−1 and 362 C g−1 with good cycling stability. Furthermore, the ASC has been fabricated with V- 
doped ZnO as a cathode and activated carbon as a negative electrode, which shows a high specific capa-
citance of 111 F g−1, an energy density of 32.4 Wh kg−1, and a power density of 5.16 kW kg−1, respectively. 
The fabricated device also demonstrated excellent electrochemical capacitance retention of 85% and 
Coulombic efficiency of 98% after 2000 cycles. These superior characteristics indicate the promising po-
tentiality of the new materials reporting for low-cost and high-performance supercapacitors.

1. Introduction 
In recent years, the increasing electrical-energy demand in day-to- 
day life raises the need for efficient energy storage device developments 
at a lower cost. Among the various types of energy storage devices, 
supercapacitors (SCs) have been considered as most efficient due to their 
extensive performance in energy sectors, including portable electronics, 
telecommunications, backup power systems, and vehicles [1–3]. Re-
cently metal oxides have been extensively used in supercapacitors as 
electrode materials. Among the metal oxides reported, zinc oxide (ZnO) 
has shown attractive electrochemical performances owing to its rela-
tively high thermal and chemical stability, good oxidation resistance, 
great biocompatibility, non-toxicity, and high conductivity [4,5]. Based 
on these properties and its wide range of nanostructures, ZnO has been 
considered a prominent material for a wide range of applications such as 
solar cells, displays, and integrated circuits [6–13], especially doped with 
transition metal oxides (V2O5, MoO3, MnO2, and CoO3) as composites, 
dopants and heterojunctions, etc., are widely used for energy storage 
devices, such as SCs. ZnO has high competency of low-temperature 
growth (typically 200–450 °C) with a wide variety of morphologies in-
cluding flower, wires, rods, and tube shape at nano-level [14–16]. The 
nanostructured morphology can exhibit significantly enhanced electro-
chemical performance due to its fast charge carrier transport, short 
diffusion path, and high number of electrochemical active sites [17–19]. 
ZnO has been shown superior pseudocapacitive performance in 
different synthesis processes or electrolyte environments by varying 
its morphology as well as microstructure. Many research groups 
have been investigating the doping of cationic or anionic elements to 
find enhanced electrochemical performances of ZnO [20,21]. Re-
cently, Fatih et al. [22] produced fluorine-doped ZnO nanoparticles 
and investigated their detailed electrochemical performance. The F- 
ZnO showed a high specific capacitance of 12.2 F g−1 besides a high 
energy density of 11.2 Wh kg−1 and a power density of 250 W kg−1.

More attention has been paid to the development of ZnO-based 
nanomaterials due to their high chemical and thermal stability, low 
cost, environmentally friendly, and easy doping. 
Generally, the morphology of ZnO nanostructures strongly depends 
on the synthesis technique and the structure of directing agents/tem-
plates used during the synthesis. Different physical and chemical tech-
niques have been reported for synthesis of doped and un-doped ZnO 
nanostructures with a wide variety of morphologies [27–30]. ZnO has 
been doped with a wide variety of elements based on the requirement of 
applications [31,32]. Doping with elements such as Mo and V can 
prompt significant changes in the physical properties of ZnO, and lead to 
the enhancement of specific capacitance, and long-term cycling perfor-
mance due to the contribution of each transition metal with high oxi-
dation states. The ionic radius of Zn2+ is 0.74 A°, whereas that of Mo6+ 
and V5+ are 0.59 A° and 0.54 A°, respectively [33]. Therefore, the sub-
stitution of Zn2+ with Mo6+ and V5+ is highly possible and expected to 
have a promising influence on the physical properties of ZnO. For ex-
ample, a very small amount of Mo doping can provide adequate free 
carriers to the host lattice and reduce the ion scattering effect because of 
the high valence difference between Mo6+ ions and substituted Zn2+ ions  
[34,35]. Also, the multiple valence states (+6, 5, 4, 3, 2) of Mo and (+5, 4, 
3, 2) of V contribute to the multiple carriers [36,37], which can enhance 
the electrical conductivity at lower resistance values, hence can be highly 
utilized for supercapacitors. 
The main aim of this study is to enhance the electrochemical 
properties of ZnO by doping with molybdenum and vanadium using 
a simple, cost-effective, and efficient technique, such as a modified 
chemical co-precipitation method (M-CCP). Among the different wet 
chemical methods, the conventional chemical co-precipitation 
method is a relatively simple, fast, and low-cost technique for the 
growth of ZnO nanostructures. However, the control over the par-
ticle size, shape, and distribution is limited in the conventional 
chemical co-precipitation method (C-CCP) due to the non-uniform 
heating and low solubility of the source materials. To overcome 
these issues, a modified chemical co-precipitation method (M-CCP) 
is utilized for the synthesis of Mo and V doped and undoped ZnO 
Lotus-flowers. The adopted method is simple, relatively low cost, 
and highly repeatable. In M-CCP, all the required chemicals were 
added into a beaker, and the top was firmly fixed with aluminum foil 
to restrict the evaporation of solvents, before being kept in a furnace 
(box type) at 100 °C for 6 h to obtain the desired nanostructured 
product. Usually, in C-CCP heat is supplied from the bottom of the 
vessel by using a hot-plate magnetic stirrer, which led to non-uni-
form heating, but in the case of M-CCP, the use of a box-type furnace 
for heating led to uniform and prompt supply of heat. Here we also 
study the reliability of ZnO lotus-flower properties and structure for 
supercapacitor applications. 
2. Experimental details 
2.1. Materials and methods 
Zinc nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO3)2.6H2O), Ammonium metava-
nadate (NH4VO3), Sodium molybdate (Na2MoO4) were purchased 
from Sigma Aldrich Co., Ltd., South Korea. Sodium hydroxide 
(NaOH, > 98%) and methanol were obtained from Daejung Co., Ltd., 
Korea. Deionized (DI) water is used to prepare all the aqueous 
solutions. Carbon black, polyvinylidene di-fluoride (PVDF), and N- 
methyl-2 pyrrolidone (NMP) were brought from Sigma Aldrich. 
Commercial activated carbon (AC) brought from Sigma Aldrich 
(CAS:7440-44-0, specific surface area 900 m2/g). The purchased 
chemicals and reagents are used without further purification be-
cause these are analytical grade. Nickel foam (1.6 mm thickness) was 
purchased from MTI Corporation (China). The Lotus-flower struc-
tures were produced by a low-cost modified co-precipitation 
method for undoped ZnO, Mo-ZnO, and V-ZnO samples. 
2.2. Synthesis of pristine ZnO, Mo-ZnO, and V-ZnO Lotus-flower-like 
structures 
In a typical procedure, the aqueous solution of zinc nitrate hex-
ahydrate (0.1 M for undoped, 0.095 M for Mo (0.005 M), and 0.095 M 
for V (0.005 M)) was magnetically stirred for 10 min (each beaker 
containing 50 ml solution of zinc nitrate hexahydrate). 0.4 M NaOH 
was dissolved in 50 ml DI water then added to the Zn aqueous so-
lution dropwise. After 10 min constant stirring, beakers have been 
tightly packed with the aluminum foil. The tightly packed beakers 
were placed in the oven at 100 °C for 6 h. After cooling to ambient 
temperature, white precipitation was obtained by centrifugation and 
washed with water and ethanol several times. The obtained white 
precipitation was dried at 80 °C for 5 h. The chemicals used in this 
synthesis process are inexpensive and abundant and it is believed 
that the modified co-precipitation method is a versatile and pow-
erful technique for the synthesis of ZnO nanomaterials. The sche-
matic synthesis process of this study is shown in Fig. 1. 
2.3. Electrodes preparation 
Electrodes preparation begins by immersing Ni foams (1.5 cm ×  
1 cm) in a concentrated Hydrochloric acid solution to remove the 
oxide layer from the surface. Ni foams were sonicated for 10 min and 
then removed from Hydrochloric acid. The Ni foams were washed 
with ethanol and deionized water using an ultra-sonicator. Then, the 
Ni foams were dried at 80 °C for 6 h. The preparation of the working 
electrode includes the mixing of active material, conductive carbon 
black, and PVDF in an 80:10:10. NMP was added to the mixture to 
form a homogenous slurry. 5 mg of this slurry was brush-coated 
onto the pre-weighed Ni substrate. The coated electrode was dried at 
85 °C for 5 h using the box furnace to remove the NMP solution. The 
coated electrode is used as a current collector. 
The electrochemical measurements are performed in an elec-
trochemical workstation (Model: CHI 760E) having 3-electrode 
system containing working electrode, counter electrode (Pt), and 
reference electrode (Ag/AgCl), whereas the active electrolyte used in 
the system is 2 M KOH solution. Finally, electrochemical measure-
ments such as Cyclic Voltammetry (CV), Galvanometric charge-dis-
charge (GCD), and Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) 
were performed. 
2.4. Asymmetric supercapacitor device fabrication 
The asymmetric supercapacitor device is made of VZO/Ni foam as 
positive, AC/Ni as the negative electrode, and sandwiched with the 
separator. Here, the cellulose filter paper is used as a separator. The 
viscous slurry was formed by grinding the AC:PVDF:carbon black at a 
mass ratio of 80:10:10 with adding an appropriate amount of NMP 
solvent in an agate mortar. The positive and the negative electrodes 
were prepared by coating the slurry on a clean Ni-substrate and 
dried at 160 °C for 4 h. Then the dry electrode was pressed to 10 MPa 
to firmly AC bond with the Ni-foam. The mass of AC coated on the 
nickel foam is valued to be 2.2 mg. Finally, electrochemical mea-
surements were performed on the asymmetric supercapacitor 
device.

tively, (JCPDS #00-036-1451). The sharp and high intense peaks of

is calculated for all samples from XRD data.

In this instance, the Mo6+ has an ionic radius of 0.59 A° and Zn2+ 
has 0.74 A°. The ionic radius of Mo6+ is smaller than the ionic radius 
of Zn2+, so Mo6+ ions can easily penetrate the ZnO lattice sites 
without affecting the ZnO crystal structure [38]. The Mo2+ (0.8 A°) 
ionic radius is larger than that of Zn2+ (0.74 A°). As a consequence, it 
is difficult to function as an interstitial impurity, but it may present 
on the ZnO surface [39]. Moreover, doping of V can decrease the ZnO 
crystal size and does not impose a significant change in crystallinity. 
A mixed state of crystalline nature of MZO Lotus-flowers has also 
exhibit typical crystalline size 16 nm for ZnO pristine. The lightening 
in crystallite sizes is owing to the resulting age of Mo-O-Zn groups 
on the surficial areas of the changed nanocomposites, prompting the 
hindrance of translucent enlargement and maturation. At room 
temperature, it is not necessarily expected to synthesize zinc oxide 
directly instead of more or less crystalline zinc hydroxide: the 
published thermodynamic data do not lead to any clear conclusions 
and do raise recurring problems [40]. Also, precipitation generally 
undergoes various transitions from amorphous hydroxide to crys-
talline hydroxide and then to oxide. In many metal ion systems, 
there is no doubt about the expected final product, whether it is 
crystalline hydroxide or oxide, but under the action of low-tem-
perature zinc salts, we will face a critical situation. Usually, the 
precipitation process uses high temperature to force the hydrolysis 
to produce ZnO, but to better understand the formation of the oxide 
phase, it is found that choosing the easiest possible conditions to 
directly precipitate zinc oxide is more instructive. In the present 
modified co-precipitation process, zinc oxide flower-structured 
product was obtained at a low temperature of 100 °C by choosing the 
required possible conditions (uniform heating). 
Raman analysis has been conducted for the analysis of crystal 
quality, structural defects, and disorder of synthesized samples. The 
ZO, MZO, and VZO samples expressed prominent Raman modes at 
333, 385−1, 437 cm−1, and 580 cm−1 (Fig. 2(b)) [41,42]. ZnO has C46v 
symmetry with two formula units in the primitive cell. The optical 
phonons correspond to the irreducible representation at the Bril-
louin zone is Γopt=A1 +E1 + 2E2 + 2B1 [43]. Transverse (TO) and 
longitudinal optical (LO) phonons, both Raman and IR active, are 
divided into the polar modes A1 and E1. Mode E2 is non-polar and is 
Raman active only. Mode B1 is Raman and IR silent, as detailed in  
[44]. Raman spectra of the ZnO samples are shown in Fig. 2(b). The 
peaks at 333 cm−1 and 437 cm−1 are attributed to E(low)2(E2l), 
multiphonon, and E(high)2(E2h) modes, respectively [42]. The 
A1(TO) mode is attributed to the peak at 385 cm−1 [42]. Never-
theless, the peak near 580 cm−1 has been attributed to the E1(LO) 
mode of ZnO [42]. However, due to Zn–O bond breakage, some au-
thors have found this peak in N-doped samples with forbidden 
scattering geometry associated with resonance-enhanced LO pho-
nons [45]. The V doped ZnO sample shows peaks at 439 and 
580 cm−1. The peak at 439 cm−1 is attributed to the E2(high) phonon 
mode of ZnO and the peak at 580 cm−1 is assigned to E1(LO) and 2 
E1(LO) modes, respectively. The observed deviation in peak positions 
compared to undoped ZnO has been explained by the difference in 
mass and the ionic radius of V and Zn ions in the lattice. The pre-
sence of strong E2 mode and weak E1(LO) mode confirms the good 
quality of the crystal with fewer structural defects and impurities. 
The vibrational atoms of oxygen in ZnO are correlated with the 
presence of strong E2 (high) mode at 439 cm−1, indicating the 
wurtzite nature of ZnO [46]. Moreover, the peak at 580 cm−1 that 
corresponds to the A1(LO) mode is originated by oxygen vacancies in 
ZnO, suggesting that Mo can induce oxygen vacancies in ZnO [46]. 
The E2(low) and E2(high) modes are attributed to the oxygen and 
zinc sublattices in ZnO, respectively, [47]. 
3.2. Morphological (FE-SEM and HR-TEM) Analysis 
The ZnO nanocrystal growth is understood by determining the 
Na+ counterions around the nanocrystals, which form a virtual 
coating that lead to a significant slowdown in growth rate and 
nonmonotonic dependence on NaOH concentration. This is different 
from the qualitative nature of NaOH and is anticipated diffusion- 
limited Ostwald ripening mechanism. In the present study, we re-
commend a new solid-solid transition mechanism to form ZnO 
Lotus-flowers from ε-Zn(OH)2 intermediate, which contrasts with 
the expected dissolution-reprecipitation process. The temperature 
and base concentration of the reaction solution plays a major role in 
the early formation of flower-shaped ZnO. Four possible dynamic 
equilibria involving the conversion between Zn(OH)42-, Zn(OH)2, and 
ZnO are defined in the following scheme:. 
The FE-SEM images of undoped and doped ZnO Lotus-flowers are 
shown in Fig. 3(a-c). From Fig. 3 inset figures, the high magnification 
FE-SEM images indicate the self-assembly of numerous irregular 
nanoparticles interwoven to form a Lotus-flower appearance. 
Fig. S1(a-c) shows the uniform growth of ZO, MZO, and VZO Lotus- 
flowers over a large area, respectively. The orientation of nano-
particles within flower-shaped particles was observed in the kinetic 
study of the reaction of zinc nitrate and sodium hydroxide by Oli-

flowers showed 3D flower-like structure with a size of ~2 µm. The Zn

iented nanoparticles. Li and Haneda et al., also grown this type of

like particles for Zn(NO3)2 and NaOH combination by microwave 
synthesis [50]. Instead, by doping with Mo and V, the process pro-
duced branching for ZnO Lotus-flowers structures. In this case, the 
reaction is less regulated by the precipitation rate and the thermo-
dynamic stability (equilibrium constants k2  >  k1) becomes the key 
factor deciding the presence of phase, so that in the initial stage no 
branched structure of ε-Zn(OH)2 will be formed directly the ZnO 
Lotus-flower shape structure. The final particles are, therefore, the 
product of the continuous growth of these materials which were 
initially created. The branching structure of ZnO is formed directly 
from the solution. In addition, the self-assembly growth and con-
trolled synthesis mechanism can be found in Yu Chang et al.’s and 
Oliveira et al.’s study [48,51]. Shi’s studies on nanocrystals formation 
under hydrothermal conditions have shown that when insoluble

3.3. Plausible formation mechanism 
Based on our resultant experimental data as well recent litera-
ture survey on the ZnO nanostructures, the underlying reaction 
mechanism to the formation of the ZnO Lotus flower has been de-
scribed [55]. Initially, the aqueous NaOH solution is produced the 
hydroxyl ions (OH˙), which easily react with Zinc metal (Zn2+) and 
then formed as the Zn(OH)42·species (Eqs. 3 & 4) [56]. Afterward, the 
ZnO nuclei are produced from the dehydration of [Zn(OH)4]2− ions 
(Eqs. 4 & 5) [57]. The reaction solution containing 0.01 M of Zn(NO3)2 
and 0.4 M of NaOH leads to an initial burst of uniform nucleation. To 
get the crystalline ZnO nanostructures after ZnO nuclei formation, 
there will be three steps undergo in the reaction medium as follows: 
(i) Initially, the resultant ZnO nuclei undergo the aggregation based 
on their electrostatic force, (ii) Later, based on the limited surface 
energy in aqueous solution at heating conditions, the molecules and 
ions of ZnO originated uniform pattern, its mean crystallization, and 
(iii) Finally, the resultant crystalline nature of ZnO has shown the 
enhanced surface active sites thereby improve the abilities to grow 
in the required orientation, which leads to the formation of various 
ZnO nanostructures (Ex. ZnO Lotus flower). The schematic re-
presentation of the ZnO Lotus flower formation mechanism is shown 
in Fig. 5(d). Therefore, the process is related to the inclusion of 
growth units on different faces, the nature of the crystal growth 
interfaces, and the structural mechanism under the influence of OH 
ions. The ZnO Lotus-flowers were created when the Zn(OH)42- ions 
concentration exceeded the critical value, and the chemical

3.4. XPS analysis 
The chemical valance of various elements and the surface com-
position on ZnO, Mo doped, and V doped ZnO were studied by XPS. 
The XPS survey spectra show the existence of Mo, V, Zn, O, and C in 
the ZnO Lotus-flowers (Fig. 6(a)). The presence of episodic hydro-
carbons in the XPS instrument and CO2 adsorbed on the sample 
surface could explain the C peak in the spectrum. Fig. 6(b) shows the 
Zn2p spectra of all the samples. The binding energy peak at 
1021.05 eV is assigned to the Zn2p3/2 peak for Zn2+ and the peak at 
1044.12 eV is assigned to the Zn2P1/2 for Zn2+. No metallic Zn was 
observed at the binding energy of 1021.50 eV, confirming the pre-
sence of Zn only in the oxidization state [59]. Fig. 6(c) presents the 
O1s spectrum of all the samples. The major peak at 531.2 eV in the 
O1s core-level spectra of MZO Lotus-flowers is deconvoluted into 
two peaks. The low binding energy peak denoted by O1 at 529.85 eV 
corresponds to the Zn-O bond, while the higher one at 530.90 eV 
(O2) is usually attributed to oxygen vacancies in ZnO [60]. To de-
termine the oxidation state of V in the as-grown VZO Lotus-flowers, 
XPS spectra of the V2p3/2 signal were obtained, as shown in Fig. 6(d). 
In the XPS spectra found on the V-doped samples, the typical V2p 
duplet peak centered at 2p3/2 can be deconvoluted into two peaks 
belonging to V5+ and V4+ at 517.1 eV. V5+ was originally existent in 
the precursor deposited on the surface of ZnO, while V4+ was formed 
during the synthesis of the Zn-O group formed during the surface 
reaction. In addition, V doped ZnO Lotus-flower in the reducing at-
mosphere of ZnO with a substantial reduction of V5+ to V4+ [45]. In 
this case, the asymmetric V2p3/2 line contains 2 peaks centered at 
514.1 eV and 516 eV (Fig. 6(d)) confirming the presence of V4+ and 
V3+, respectively [46]. No additional contributions from V2+ and V4+ 
valence states were noticed in any of the examined samples. 
Therefore, their existence can be excluded within the detection limit 
of XPS. Individually, the V dopant is mostly present in the V3+ va-
lence state. The XPS spectrum of Mo3d is deconvoluted into two 
separate peaks located at the binding energy of 232.44 and 
235.46 eV corresponding to the Mo3d5/2 and Mo3d3/2, respectively, 
as displayed in Fig. 6(e) [39,40]. The peak separation of 3 eV in-
dicates that the elemental Mo4+ exists as Mo6+ in molybdates. The 
Mo3d XPS spectrum (Fig. 6(e)) shows a peak at approximately 
235.25 eV corresponding to Mo3d3/2 [61]. The Mo6+ observed on the 
doped surface at.1.5% is the outcome of surface oxidation, which can 
be found in previous reports on Mo-doped metal oxides [62,63]. 
Although difficulty in Mo oxidation state confirmation, the presence 
of Mo4+ on the surface despite surface oxidation and the fact that 
Zn2+ (0.6 Å) ionic radius is more consistent with Mo4+ (0.65 Å) than 
with Mo6+ (0.41 Å) suggest that Mo is in the + 4 oxidation state.

The electrochemical performance of VZO, MZO and ZO electrodes 
was studied in a 3-electrode configuration. The results of CV curves 
confirm faradaic redox reaction and show the battery type behavior 
of the electrode materials. Fig. 7(a) presents a typical CV of the ZO, 
MZO, and VZO electrodes at a scan rate of 100 mV s−1. The VZO ex-
hibits a larger area under the curve than ZO and MZO, which in-
dicates that more energy is stored in the electroactive sites of the 
VZO electrode compared to ZO and MZO [64]. Fig. S2 (a1, a2, a3) 
(supporting information) shows the CV curves for all electrodes at 
different scan rates of 10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 175, and 
200 mV s−1 with a potential window of − 0.4–0.9 V. At higher scan 
rates, a smaller surface response was detected due to the limited 
time. Nevertheless, the ions have enough time to react, resulting in 
enhanced charge storage at low scan rates. These findings indicate 
that the specific capacity is higher at low scan rates [65]. The fast 
ions/electrons kinetic and rapid redox reactions at the electrode/ 
electrolyte interface can facilitate shifts in the oxidation peak along 
with the higher potential due to enough time to interact with each 
other and reduction peaks in the lower potential for higher scan

[66]. It is also interesting to note that at high scan rates, the shape 
profile of the CV curves does not change, indicating superior capa-
citive behavior. Moreover, it can also be seen that the current of each 
CV curve is increased with an increasing scan rate. This aspect may

The kinetic properties of the electrodes were analyzed by EIS 
measurements. Fig. 7(d) displays the Nyquist plots of all the samples 
from low-to-high frequency regions. According to the Nyquist plot, 
the curve can be divided into three segments. The electrolyte re-
sistance (Rs) (ionic resistance of the electrolyte + intrinsic resistance 
of the electrode + interface resistance) is represented by the inter-
section with the x-axis in the high-frequency region [70]. The charge 
transfer resistance (Rct) is proportional to the diameter of the 
semicircle [71]. The slope of the straight line in the low-frequency 
zone displays the diffusion resistance, which is connected to the 
diffusion of OH- in alkaline electrodes [72]. From Fig. 7(d), the 
semicircular part is decreased from ZO to VZO, which indicates that 
the Rct value of the electrode is low. And in line with the CV and GCD 
results, in this case, compared with other samples, VZO also showed 
the best supercapacitive performance on the smallest semicircular 
part. The small (or almost negligible) semicircular part of VZO in-
dicates that the charge transfer resistance is negligible. This is due to 
the low Faradaic resistance of the electrodes [73], so it can reiterate 
its excellent pseudocapacitance characteristics. In addition, the 
lower inset of Fig. 7(d) displays the magnified version of the high- 
frequency intercepts of the curves at the real axis, which represents 
a very small value, indicating the equivalent series resistance Rs of 
the electrode. 
The inset of Fig. 7(d) shows EIS data with standard equivalent 
circuit {Rs + CPE||(Rct + W)}. The real part (Zr) in the high-frequency 
region is attributed to the equivalent series resistance (ESR). The ESR 
of VZO, MZO, and ZnO electrode materials are 0.86, 1.54, and 1.77 Ω, 
respectively, indicating that the ohmic loss is very small during 
discharge. The Warburg impedance (W) of VZO, MZO, and ZO elec-
trodes are 6.42, 17.45, and 39.63 Ω, respectively. W is related to the 
diffusion of OH- ions generated by the reaction in the electrolyte  
[74]. The VZO electrode exhibits the largest slope than other elec-
trodes, indicating the faster ion diffusion rate. The Rct and Rs of the 
VZO electrode are shown to be lower than those of other electrodes, 
which indicates that the VZO electrode has high conductivity and 
superior supercapacitive performance compared with other elec-
trodes, thus corroborating the CV and GCD data.

5. Conclusions 
In summary, metal ions, including Mo and V doped ZnO Lotus- 
flowers were synthesized by a facile chemical co-precipitation 
method for the fabrication of high-performance supercapacitors. 
Among the materials synthesized, the VZO electrode with a Lotus- 
flower-like morphology showed good battery type behavior with 
high specific capacities. The electrochemical performance of the best 
performing VZO electrode showed a maximum specific capacity of 
362 C g−1 with an excellent capacity retention of 88% after 10,000 
charge/discharge cycles. The best-performing electrode was used to 
fabricated an ASC device that showed the highest specific capaci-
tance of 111 F g−1 with an energy density of 32.4 Wh kg−1 and power 
density of 5.16 kW kg−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1. Also, the de-
vice exhibited capacity retention of 85% and Coulombic efficiency of 
98% over 2000 cycles at a current density of 8 A g−1, indicating su-
perior reversibility and device stability. These results indicate that 
high-efficiency supercapacitor electrode VZO is a promising mate-
rial, and the application of V-ZnO-based electrodes can be greatly 
extended to other high-efficiency energy storage systems.

An efficient biosynthesis of palladium nanoparticles using Bael gum and 
evaluation of their catalytic and antibacterial activity

ABSTRACT  
We report a facile microwave-assisted synthesis of palladium nanoparticles (PdNPs) using Bael gum (BG) and it's 
carboxymethylated (CMBG) derivative. The prepared nanoparticles (BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs) were 
evaluated for antibacterial and catalytic activity in the reduction of organic dye pollutants. The developed 
synthetic method is simple, low cost and eco-friendly, wherein the process requires no additional reducing or 
capping agents. The CMBG was prepared via etherification reaction between BG and monochloroacetic acid 
using Williamson synthesis method. The PdNPs were synthesized using BG and CMBG as stabilizers and reducing 
agents. The PdNPs were found to be well dispersed spherical, with the crystalline size of the order of 7–21 nm. 
The results showed that the CMBG@PdNPs were smaller in size (7 ± 2 nm) than those capped with BG@PdNPs 
(10 ± 2 nm). The catalytic ability of CMBG@PdNPs was examined for the reduction of Methyl Orange (MO), 
Methyl Red(MR), and Rhodamine-B (RhB) in the presence of NaBH4. The results showed that CMBG@PdNPs 
exhibited a higher catalytic ability than BG@PdNPs. Moreover, it was found that CMBG@PdNPs served several 
times as a retrievable and reusable catalyst which is stable even after six cycles of reaction. The CMBG@PdNPs 
and BG@PdNPs showed excellent antibacterial activity. The results indicate that CMBG@PdNPs have greater 
potential application as a catalyst in the reduction of organic pollutants and antibacterial activity.   
1. Introduction 
Nanotechnology and Nanoscience have emerged as a saviour for 
current generation problems. The applications of nanotechnology have 
set their roots in all areas of science and technology, stretching from the 
basic human needs like food and medicine to global issues, i.e., energy, 
pollution control, and remediation. The need for quality food has led the 
scientific community, government organizations, and industries to 
search for new products and protocols based on nanotechnology [1,2]. 
Nanotechnology has provided a sophisticated and multi-disciplinary 
approach to drug designing and drug delivery which has revolution-
ized the whole medical research field [3]. Recently, nanotechnology has 
played a significant role in the development of transition metal oxides 
nanocomposites with different dimensions as an electrode for high 
performance supercapacitor [4,5]. 
Nowadays, pigments and dyes are found in many industrial effluents 
discharged by textiles, cosmetics, leather, paper, food, and other 
chemical processing industries. Dye-contaminated industrial effluents 
cause adverse effects on the environment as well as human health due to 
their highly toxic nature. Dye pollutants are highly carcinogenic and 
chemically more stable [6]. These dyes cannot be easily degraded to 
nontoxic products and cause adverse effects such as liver and kidney 
damage, a blood disorder, central nervous system poisoning, and skin 
irradiation [6]. Catalytic reduction of organic dyes using metal nano-
particles is an interesting subject due to its high efficacy [6]. Engineered 
nanomaterials have provided a novel approach to the remediation of 
pollution and its effects. Nanomaterials can effectively remove the pol-
lutants from soil and groundwater [7]. Some other catalysts or adsor-
bents have been reported for organic pollutants treating polluted water 
[8]. The nanomaterials have shown great potential in addressing many

of our current generation problems due to their size, structure, speci-
ficity, and versatility [9,10]. Therefore, more and more researchers and 
scientists have started searching for solutions in nanotechnology for 
problems in their field. 
Nanomaterials are generally classified depending on the material as 
metal-based nanoparticles, carbon-based nanoparticles, organic 
compound-based nanoparticles, and composite-based nanoparticles. 
They all display unique properties due to their size, morphology, 
composition, and agglomeration. Among all, metal nanoparticle-based 
materials are very special due to their diverse applications ranging 
from mechanical optical to biomedical [11]. In recent years, nano-
structures of gold, silver, and platinum are being widely studied in the 
biomedical field, leading to their clinical use [8,12,13]. Researchers 
have shown renewed interest and attention towards the Noble palla-
dium nanoparticles (PdNPs) due to their high chemical and thermal 
stability [14,15], non-toxicity, high surface area, and its use in several 
organic reactions as a catalyst like hydrogenation reaction, Suzuki 
coupling, Heck C–C coupling [16], reduction of toxic organic com-
pounds [17]. 
PdNPs are being tried as photothermal agents in photothermal 
therapy [18], photoacoustic agents in photoacoustic imaging for early 
detection of tumors [19], efficient nanocarriers for genes and drugs 
[20], and as prodrug activators [21]. The specific surface and pore size 
distribution of the palladium nanoparticles may influence the catalysis 
properties [17]. Furthermore, PdNPs have been tested on several cancer 
cell lines [22] and also as antimicrobial agents on several bacterial 
strains [23]. The interesting application of PdNPs comes in the form of 
nanostructured Pd microelectrodes generated by electrodeposition 
methods as nanoscale biosensors for high-performance diagnostic tools 
in medicine [24]. In addition to the above applications, PdNPs are also 
being used for organic synthesis [25], hydrogen storage/sensing [26], 
fuel cells [27] and catalytic reduction of organic dyes. 
The synthesis of PdNPs has been reported by diverse techniques [28], 
such as thermal decomposition, chemical reduction, and vapour depo-
sition [29]. However, all these synthetic methods have used either 
expensive and toxic chemicals or required high energy. In recent years, 
researchers have shown much attention to the green synthesis of PdNPs 
due to its cost-effectiveness, simplicity, biocompatibility, and non- 
toxicity [30]. Recently researchers have been reported less toxic and 
highly biocompatibility palladium metal nanoparticles for biological 
and catalytic applications [31–33]. Herein, we report a facile biosyn-
thesis of PdNPs in an aqueous medium using BG and CMBG. Gums are 
natural polymers obtained from marine, plant, and microbial sources. 
The gum from plant sources comes either from seeds, tree exudates, 
tubers, and extracts. Gums from different plant sources were being used 
as food and in traditional medicine [34,35]. The gum obtained from 
plants contains various bioactive phytochemicals. It is being used in 
medicine, pharmacology, agriculture, environmental and chemical en-
gineering [36]. Due to their excellent biocompatibility, biodegrad-
ability, nontoxicity, and easy accessibility, several gums have been used 
to prepare medical systems and devices such as wound healing dress-
ings, drug delivery, and artificial tissue engineering scaffolding systems 
[37]. The green synthesis of metal nanoparticles has improved their 
application in medicine due to their biocompatible and improved effi-
cacy as compared to physical and chemical methods [38]. 
Globally, antimicrobial drug resistance has become one of the most 
significant public health concerns. Microbial infections cause about 3 
million deaths annually in developing countries. Most of the deaths due 
to microbial infections occur in tropical countries despite vast advances 
in diagnosis and treatment [39]. An estimated $20 billion dollars is the 
economic cost of multidrug-resistant (MDR) microbes in the U.S. alone 
[40]. Due to resistance, clinicians are frequently left with no reliable 
alternative to manage infected patients. As a result, MDR and exten-
sively drug-resistant (XDR) bacteria are a significant public health 
concern since they are associated with high mortality, morbidity, and 
treatment costs [41,42]. A promising therapeutic strategy for microbes 
is nanotechnology by virtue of its high efficacy and therapeutic index 
[43]. Most bacterial infections can be effectively treated with nano-
particles, especially those involving multi-drug resistant bacteria. Using 
nanoparticles along with antibiotics provide excellent synergistic 
effects. 
Bael, Aegle marmelos (L.) Corrˆea is also known as begal-quince, 
golden apple, and stone apple is one of the medicinal plant species 
grown in India [44]. It ine of the medicinally important plants 
mentioned in a renowned ayurvedic medical book called Charaka 
Samhita [45]. Various parts of the plant are used in ayurvedic and folk 
medicine as a remedy for different ailments [46]. The fruit and seeds of 
the plant are used in the treatment of neurological problems, mal- 
absorption, dysentery, edema, dyspepsia, etc. [44]. Beal is also used in 
food processing and extraction of economically important herbal com-
pounds. Green synthesis of gold nanoplates using BG as a capping agent 
has been reported [47]. The Bael gum has been found to improve chi-
tosan's film-forming property, and the resulting film showed improved 
mechanical and electrochemical properties [48]. The PdNPs have been 
synthesized using various gums derived from plant sources [49,50]. 
Earlier, our team has reported the synthesis and application of metal 
nanoparticles capped with natural and modified gums [51–53]. 
Considering the medical applications and renewed interest of re-
searchers in preparing biogenic nanomaterial, especially from natural 
gums, motivated us to prepare PdNPs from readily available and low- 
cost material BG and to study its applications. Moreover, a review of 
the literature shows no report of the synthesis of PdNPs using bael gum 
and its applications. 
Based on the current study, we report the synthesis of PdNPs using 
Bael gum (BG) and CMBG. The CMBG was characterized in terms of 
chemical and physical properties using FTIR, TGA, DSC, XRD, and SEM 
techniques. BG and CMBG stabilized PdNPs were characterized using 
FTIR, XRD, DLS, SEM, and TEM techniques. The antimicrobial proper-
ties of BG and CMBG stabilized PdNPs were studied. The catalytic effi-
cacy of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs was assessed by exploring their 
ability with Methyl Orange (MO), Methyl Red (MR), Rhodamine-B 
(RhB) dyes, and antibacterial activity were tested. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Materials 
BG was purchased from the Girijana Cooperative Society of Telan-
gana, India. Sodium tetrachloropalladate and dyes were purchased from 
Sigma-Aldrich and other chemicals were purchased from Sd fine chem 
limited, Mumbai, India. All the microbial test strains were procured 
from the IMTECH Laboratory, Chandigarh, India. 
2.2. Carboxymethylation of Bael gum 
CMBG was prepared by mixing the collected BG (1g) with 5 mL of 
distilled water, followed by the addition of 95 mL of ice-cold NaOH 
solution (55% w/v). About 10 mL of monochloroacetic acid (75%, w/v) 
solution was slowly added over 10 min to the above reaction mixture. 
The temperature of the reaction mixture was gradually increased up to 
65 ◦C and stirred for 2 h. The pH of the suspension was neutralized with 
glacial acetic acid. The obtained wet solid mass was washed with 
methanol and dried in an oven at 50–65 ◦C [54]. 
2.3. Synthesis of PdNPs with BG 
BG (0.5 g) was dispersed in 50 mL of double distilled water with 
stirring for 2 h at 60 ◦C, cooled, and filtered by using Whatman filter 
paper to get a clear solution. To synthesize BG-capped PdNPs, 5 mL of 1 
mM Na2PdCl4 and 10 mL of 1% BG solution were taken in a beaker. The 
reaction mixture was irradiated with Microwave (MWI) at 750 W for 3 
min. The resulting reaction mixture showed a grey color indicating the

formation of PdNPs. 
2.4. Synthesis of PdNPs with CMBG 
CMBG (0.5 g) was dispersed in 50 mL of double distilled water with 
stirring for 1 h at 60 ◦C, cooled, and filtered by using Whatman filter 
paper to get a clear solution. To synthesize CMBG capped PdNPs, 5 mL of 
1 mM Na2PdCl4 and 10 mL of 1% CMBG solution were taken in a beaker. 
The reaction mixture was subjected to MWI for 3 min at 750 W. The 
resulting reaction mixture showed a grey color indicating the formation 
of PdNPs. 
2.5. Characterization techniques 
Various physicochemical characterization techniques have been 
used to determine the formation of CMBG, BG@PdNPs, and 
CMBG@PdNPs. The morphology of BG and CMBG was examined using 
SEM (Carl Zeiss SEM with the Oxford EDX attachment, at O⋅U). DSC and 
TGA analysis were carried out on STA7200 thermal analysis system, 
Hitachi was used to perform DSC and TGA studies. The UV-visible 
spectra were recorded on UV-3200, Shimadzu, Japan. FTIR spectra 
were carried out using Shimadzu IR Affinity-1. The powder XRD was 
analyzed by using Rigaku Miniflex. TEM (JEOL2000) was used to 
measure the size and morphology of the synthesized BG@PdNPs and 
CMBG@PdNPs and SEM were investigated with the ZEISS EVO instru-
ment. The Zeta potential of the PdNPs was determined using DLS 
(Malvern instrument Ltd). 
2.6. Catalytic reduction of dyes 
The synthesized BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs were tested for 
catalytic activity for the reduction of MO, MR, and RhB dyes in the 
presence of NaBH4. About 1.5 mL of 0.5 mM MO solution, 1 mL of 10 
mM NaBH4, and 10 mL of double distilled water were stirred for 5 min. 
3 mL of the reaction mixture was taken into a cuvette, and 5 mg of PdNPs 
were added. The catalytic reduction studies were carried out using the 
UV–Vis Spectrophotometer. A similar approach was used for the cata-
lytic reduction of MR and RhB dyes. 
2.7. Antibacterial activity of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs 
The antibacterial activity of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs were 
tested by using the disc diffusion method. The transferred nutrient agar 
medium was allowed to solidify in the sterilized Petri dishes. 100 mL of 
bacterial suspension was transferred into mediated sterilized Petri 
dishes and incubated at 37 ◦C for 24 h in an incubator and the formed 
zone of inhibition was measured. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Characterization of CMBG 
Fig.S1 shows the FTIR spectra of BG and CMBG in the range of 
4000–400 cm� 1. The FTIR spectra of BG (pure gum) showed a broad 
absorption peak at 3390 cm� 1 was attributed to -OH stretching vibra-
tions. The bands observed at 1700, 1510, 1470, 1250, and 1030 cm� 1 
were due to the -C=O functional group, polyphenyl skeletal (aromatic), 
symmetric stretching of the C-O-C group, stretching vibrations of C–N 
amide, and C–O stretching vibrations of carboxylic acid respectively. 
The IR spectrum of CMBG showed a band at 3400–3250 cm� 1 due to 
overlapping contributions of free and bonded OH groups of carboxylic 
acid. The absorptions bands at 1750, 1260, and 700 cm� 1 were due to 
-C=O stretching vibrations, C-O-C symmetric stretching vibrations, and 
C–O wagging, respectively. The absorption bands at 1625, 1450 cm� 1 
were due to COO� asymmetric stretching vibrations of carboxylate ion 
and, while the C–O stretch of carboxylic acid appeared at 1050 cm� 1. 
The observed bands of CMBG confirmed the carboxymethylation of BG 
[47,55]. Fig.S2 shows the X-ray diffraction pattern of BG and CMBG. The 
XRD of BG did not show any peaks, indicating an amorphous nature of 
the material. Whereas XRD of CMBG shows the typical characteristic 
peaks at 2θ equal to 13.10, 14.85, 20.40, 21.50, 26.10, 28.20, 32.00, 
36.10, 41.01, and 47.15 degrees, which indicates an increase in the 
crystallinity of BG on carboxymethylation [56]. 
The differential thermogravimetric curves of BG and CMBG are 
shown in Fig. S3. The TGA analysis of mass% versus temperature 
showed that there are significant regions of mass loss within the thermal 
curves of these gums. The presence of different components with 
different structures gums cause them to exhibit different thermal 
behaviour, which is evident from their TGA curves. For the BG (black 
line), there are two significant regions of mass loss as observed in the 
TGA curve of the gum. The region of mass loss of ~20% within the 
temperature range 20–150 ◦C due to the moisture traces present in the 
gum and the second moss loss of 40% between 200 and 400 ◦C, repre-
sents the degradation of the polymer backbone. For the CMBG (redline), 
there are four significant regions of mass loss as observed in the TGA 
curve of the CMBG. The region of mass loss of ~20% within the tem-
perature range of 20–100 ◦C, 20% in the range of 250–350 ◦C, ~10% in 
the range of 450–600 ◦C and of 35% in the range of 600–750 ◦C. The 
zone of mass loss at 450–600 ◦C is due to the degradation of carbox-
ymethyl groups incorporated in the BG. The study showed that CMBG is 
thermally more stable as compared to that of BG. The yield at 800 ◦C for 
the gum (black line) was higher (~17.5%) than that of CMBG (~16%) 
(red line). These results confirmed the carboxymethylation of BG [51]. 
The DSC thermograms of BG and CMBG are shown in Fig.S4. DSC 
thermogram of BG shows a small broad endothermic peak at 45 ◦C and a 
broad endothermic peak at 278 ◦C. The thermal curves of CMBG showed 
a small broad endothermic peak at 53 ◦C and a broad endothermic peak 
at 290 ◦C. The shifting of endothermic peaks in CMBG was evidence of 
carboxymethyl group insertion in the BG. Fig.S5 shows the SEM images 
of BG and CMBG. The BG showed amorphous like images with different 
shapes. The SEM morphology of CMBG showed crystalline rods and 
stones-like images, due to the carboxymethylation of BG. All the afore-
said characterizations confirmed that the Bael gum was 
carboxymethylated. 
3.2. Properties of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs 
The synthesized BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs were characterized 
using UV-visible Spectrophotometry, FTIR, powder XRD, DLS, and TEM 
techniques. 
3.2.1. UV-visible spectroscopic studies 
The formation of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs were studied by 
using a UV-visible spectrophotometer. The pale yellow color of Pd 2+ ion 
changes into black by the addition of BG and CMBG, which indicates the 
formation of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs by reduction of Pd 2+ to 
Pd0. The UV-visible spectra of BG, Na2PdCl2 solution, BG @PdNPs, and 
CMBG@PdNPs were shown in Fig. 1. BG shows a characteristic peak at 
260 nm, Pd2+ ions showed a peak at 430 nm, whereas the BG@PdNPs 
and CMBG@PdNPs did not show any specific wavelength maximum in 
the spectra. Notably, the intensity of Pd(II) precursor absorption peaks 
will be diminished after its reduction to Pd(0). This confirmed the 
absence of Pd2+ ions in the solution of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs 
and indicated that all the Pd2+ ions were reduced to Pd0. The UV-visible 
absorption spectra confirmed the formation of BG@PdNPs and 
CMBG@PdNPs [53]. 
3.2.2. FTIR spectroscopic studies 
Fig. 2 shows the FTIR spectra of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs. The 
spectra of BG@PdNPs showed a strong peak at 3365 cm-1, corresponding 
to the -OH group. The characteristic bands at 1680, 1280, 1045, and 
880 cm� 1 were due to -C=O, -C-H, C–O, and -CH2 groups. The FTIR

Stability studies of PdNPs are essential for chemical and biological 
applications. The stability studies of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs 
were investigated by monitoring with zeta potential. Fig. 4 shows the

CMBG@PdNPs, respectively. The zeta potential study indicates that 
PdNPs are covered with the -ve charged groups like carboxyl and hy-
droxyl groups. Therefore, the synthesized BG@PdNPs and

3.2.5. Transmission electron microscopic studies 
The TEM images of synthesized BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs are 
shown in Fig. 5. The Fig. 5a shows that the BG stabilized PdNPs were

protected the PdNPs (BG@PdNPs) from aggregation [51]. The histo-

Fig. 5c shows that the CMGK@PdNPs were spherical in shape with a 
smooth surface. The average particle size distribution histogram is 
drawn by counting about 100 PdNPs (Fig. 5d). The mean size of the 
PdNPs was found to be 7 ± 2 nm. The TEM images CMBG@PdNPs

3.3. Mechanism of BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs formation 
The synthesized BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs were characterized 
using several physiochemical characterization techniques. According to 
FTIR, the BG shows the presence of several functional groups such as 
hydroxyl, amino, carboxyl, and carbonyl groups. The modified BG 
contains a -CH2COOH group along with the other functional groups. 
Under microwave irradiation, the functional groups of BG bound with 
the Pd2+ ions and reduced them to PdNPs, further preventing their ag-
gregation. Whereas the CMBG of - CH2COOH groups bound with the 
Pd2+ ions and rapidly reduced them to PdNPs and further prevented 
them from aggregation. In the FTIR spectra of BG and BG@PdNPs, the 
shifting of N–H /O-H and C––O peaks 3390–3365, 1680–1700 cm� 1, 
respectively, indicated the formation of BG@PdNPs. In the FTIR spectra 
of CMBG and CMBG@PdNPs, the shifting of N-H/O-H and C––O peaks 
3400–3375, 1750–1720 cm� 1 respectively indicated the formation of 
CMBG@PdNPs [53]. 
As these functional groups are complex in nature, it was confirmed 
by FTIR wherein it was noticed that hydroxyl, carbonyl, and carboxylic 
groups had strong affinities for binding with palladium ions in order to 
form a protective surface layer around the PdNPs that stops aggregation. 
A possible nanoparticle formation mechanism is presented in Fig. 6.

Many chemists have been using NaBH4 as a strong reducing agent for

concentrations of MO dye by the reduction reaction. Catalytic reduction 
efficiency of BG @ PdNPs and CMBG @ PdNPs were assessed using MO 
dye in the presence of NaBH4. Initially, the UV-visible spectra of MO dye

absorption peaks at 340 and 465 nm. MO dye reduction studies were 
performed by using NaBH4, but there is no noticeable change in the peak

MR dye is used as an indicator in chemical analysis in the laboratory

cause respiratory tract infection and gastrointestinal digestion problems. 
Sustainable technologies are essential for the degradation of MR dyes 
without harming the environment. Catalytic reduction efficacy of BG @ 
PdNPs and CMBG @ PdNPs were tested using MR dye in the presence of 
NaBH4. Initially, the UV-visible absorption spectra of MR dye were 
recorded for reference. The electronic spectra of MR dye showed an 
absorption maximum at 530 nm (π – π*). The catalytic reduction of MR 
dye was evaluated using BG@PdNPs. MR dye reduction studies were 
initially performed using NaBH4 catalyst, but there is no noticeable 
change in the peak intensity even after 15 min. It concludes that the MR

examined by using MR dye in the presence of NaBH4. The reduction of

3.4.4. Catalytic mechanism of BG@PdNPs/CMBG@PdNPs 
From the aforesaid results, it was found that the reduction of dyes in 
the presence of NaBH4 was completely negligible. But in the presence of 
BG@PdNPs/CMBG@PdNPs and NaBH4, a rapid reduction of dyes was 
observed. From these observations, it is concluded BG@PdNPs and 
CMBG@PdNPs act as good catalysts for the reduction of MO, MR, and 
RhB dyes. Based on this, a reasonable mechanism is proposed for the 
reduction of the dyes (Fig. 10). In the presence of palladium nano-
particles (BG@PdNPs/CMBG@PdNPs), both BH4� ions and dye mole-
cules are absorbed together on the surface of PdNPs [53]. Through 
electrostatic interaction, PdNPs play a key role in the transfer of elec-
trons from BH4� (donor) to the analytes (accepter) and all these reactions 
happen at the surface of PdNPs. As a result of the electron transfer, the 
dyes will be reduced at the surface of PdNPs [38]. Finally, the formed 
products are desorbed from the surface of the PdNPs and diffuse out into 
the bulk of the solution.

3.4.5. Recyclability of CMBG@PdNPs catalysts 
The recyclability of a catalyst is an important requirement in any 
catalytic reaction [74]. The recovery and reuse of CMBG@PdNPs cata-
lysts were examined for several cycles of MO, MR, and RhB reduction 
processes. The nanoparticles were recovered from the reaction mixture 
after the end of the reaction. The recovered PdNPs were washed with 
water and ethanol, dried in a vacuum oven, and used for the next cycle 
[60]. The result of reusable PdNPs catalysts for the reduction of MO is 
shown in Fig. S9. The PdNPs exhibited little loss even after six cycles. 
Similarly, the recycling ability of PdNPs for the reduction reaction of MR 
and RhB is shown in Figs. S10 and S11, respectively. The PdNPs exhibit 
very little catalytic activity loss even after six cycles and high stability. 
3.5. Antibacterial property of CMBG@PdNPs 
Antibacterial activity of CMBG@PdNPs was examined against gram- 
negative and gram-positive bacteria [75]. The antibacterial activity was 
determined by the disc diffusion method [44]. The formed zone of in-
hibitions for CMBG@PdNPs are listed in Table 1. The different con-
centrations of PdNPs such as 100, 200, and 300 μL were used (Fig. 11). 
The zone of inhibition for Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Escherichia coli 
were 20 ± 0.3 and 21 ± 0.5. Whereas, Bacillus subtilis and Bacillus 
megaterium showed the zone of inhibition of 19 ± 0.5 and 18 ± 0.3. The 
CMBG@PdNPs showed an excellent antibacterial activity towards the 
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Escherichia coli and moderate activity 
against Bacillus subtilis and Bacillus megaterium. The antibacterial activity 
of increases with the increasing concentration of CMBG @PdNPs. These 
results conclude that the CMBG@PdNPs have good antibacterial activ-
ity. These results suggest that CMBG@PdNPs could be used as a good 
antimicrobial agent in biomedical applications.

catalyst for the treatment of wastewater and industrial effluents 
contaminated by organic pollutants. These results suggest that both 
BG@PdNPs and CMBG@PdNPs could be used as good antimicrobial 
agents in biomedical applications.

abstract
Copper doped zinc sulphide nanopowders (ZnS: Cu NPs) were synthesized using chemical co-
precipitation technique. The Cu-doping content in the NPs was varied in the range, 0–4 wt%. The undoped
and Cu-doped ZnS nanoparticles were prepared at 70 /C176C and dried at low temperatures. The prepared
powders were investigated to understand the structure, surface topography, optical and photolumines-
cence (PL) properties using appropriate techniques. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) studies of prepared
NPs revealed the (1 1 1) plane as the dominant orientation related to the cubic structure of ZnS. Also,
XRD spectra exhibited broadening of the crystal planes on increasing Cu-content in the starting solution.
The topography studied revealed a change from granular shaped crystals to ﬂower shaped surface mor-
phology upon Cu-doping. From the optical absorption studies, it was noted that increase of Cu-doping in
the starting solution, shifted the absorption edge toward the smaller wavelength. The band gap energy of
the NPs was evaluated by using Tauc plots, which varied from 3.7 eV to 4.1 eV with increase of Cu-doping.
The PL studies indicated a small peak at 440 nm in pure ZnS and large peak at 522 nm that are related to
the characteristic bands of ZnS. The properties of ZnS: Cu NPs were analysed for their suitability for
mono-grain solar cell application.

1. Introduction
Chalcogenide semiconductors have gained much interest over
the last several decades because of excellent physical and chemical
properties, which make them ideal for the development of many
optoelectronic and photoluminescent devices. ZnS is an important
semiconductor of this group that has a large energy gap of 3.68 eV,
high optical transmittance and good luminescence emission [1–5].
The research on ZnS nanopowders (NPs) is more attracting because
of the quantum conﬁnement effect that shoots up the band gap.
Many transition elements like Ag, Cu, Mn and others used in liter-
ature as dopants to alter the characteristics ZnS NPs to suite for
speciﬁc application. Doped ZnS NPs exhibited interesting optical
properties, particularly the decay time and emission spectra of
doped layers differing from un-doped samples. Among all the tran-
sition metal dopants, Cu 2+ is one of the strongest dopants to inter-
act with the ZnS host lattice. Cu-doped ZnS (ZnS: Cu) powder gives
many emissions over a wide spectral range. Further, the literature
reports indicated that doping of ZnS with Cu resulted in shifting of
the absorption edge to visible region so that Cu-doped ZnS
becomes a strong luminescent material.
There are many deposition methods used in the literature to
prepare ZnS ﬁlms. These include hydrothermal synthesis [6], sol–
gel process [7], co-precipitation method [8], wet chemical tech-
nique [9], microwave-assisted synthesis [10], micro-emulsion
method [11] that were used for the preparation of pure and ZnS:
Cu NPS with various morphological features. ZnS:Cu NPs were
made by Srivastava [12] et al. using zinc acetate, cupric acetate,
and sodium sulphide as precursors for Zn, Cu, and S, respectively,
at room temperature. They also studied the effect of copper con-
centration on the photoconductivity characteristics of heat-
treated ZnS nanopowders prepared using the chemical co-
precipitation technique. Pooja Dwivedi [13] et al. investigated the
impact of annealing temperature on the ferromagnetic properties
of ZnS: Cu nanoparticles. In their studies, they used zinc acetate,

of Cu-doped ZnS NPs at room temperature, prepared by chemical

Sreenivasulu et al. [16] investigated the luminescence properties of

The literature review on ZnS nanoparticles revealed that in
most of the studies either expensive techniques or time-
consuming process such as hydrothermal method, sol–gel process,
and wet chemical method etc. have been used to synthesize ZnS:
Cu nanopowders. However, in the present work, a simple and eco-
nomic chemical co-precipitation method was used. Further, the lit-
erature review also revealed that ZnS: Cu nano-powders have been
prepared using co-precipitation method with zinc acetate as a pre-
cursor for Zn and sodium sulphide as a precursor for S, whereas
either copper chloride or copper acetate was used for Cu-doping
as precursor. Some of these studies also used capping agents dur-
ing the synthesis. However, in the present work, copper sulphate
was used as Cu precursor and triethanolamine (TEA) as a complex-
ion agent to synthesize ZnS: Cu nanopowders. Furthermore, in
some studies, the ZnS nano-powders have synthesized at room
temperature, but further processed (dried) at higher temperatures
(>150 /C176C). However, in the current work, the powders were pre-
pared at 70 /C176C and dried at 70 /C176C rather than higher temperatures
as mentioned in the literature that could be more economical. In
addition, the structural, topographical and optical properties of
the ZnS: Cu powders were reported in relation to their Cu-doping
content.
2. Experimental details
2.1. Chemicals used
All analytical grade zinc acetate (Zn(CH 3CO2)2), sodium sul-
phide (Na 2S) and copper sulphate (CuSO 4) were taken as the pre-
cursors for Cu, Zn, and S respectively to prepare the starting
solutions. Triethanolamine (TEA) was used as the complexion
agent with deionized water as solvent.
2.2. Preparation of nanopowders
Zinc acetate was dissolved in double deionized water to prepare
0.01 M Zn-precursor solution. To prepare 0.01 M S-precursor solu-
tion, sodium sulphide was dissolved in deionized water. Initially,
1 ml of TEA was added to the Zn-precursor solution and heated
to 70 /C176C for 10 min with constant stirring. S-precursor solution
was added to the Zn-precursor solution slowly drop by drop. The
color of the reaction bath was changed to white with the formation
of prepcipitate. The reaction bath was heated and stirred for 2 h
before being cooled to room temperature. Finally, the reaction mix-
ture was centrifuged and thoroughly washed with ethanol and
deionized water. The entire reaction mixture was then placed in
a vacuum oven and dried for 2 h at 70 /C176C. To make Cu-doped ZnS
nanoparticles, copper sulphate was added to the reaction bath. In
relation to Cu-doing, the prepared powders were labelled as CZS
Pure (0 wt%), CZS1 (1 wt%), CZS2 (2 wt%), CZS3 (3 wt%), and CZS4
(4 wt%). The preparation of ZnS: Cu (0 – 4 wt%) nanopowders using
chemical co-precipitation method is depicted in Fig. 1 .
2.3. Characterization of nano powders
The prepared pure and doped ZnS NPs were characterized to
investigate the structure and morphology, optical and photolumi-
nescent behavior using appropriate techniques. The structural
properties were investigated by using RIGAKU; Miniﬂex-600 make
X-ray diffractometer with Cu K a radiation (k = 1.5406 Å). The mor-
phological studies were made with Carl Zeiss EVO MA 15 scanning
electron microscopy. The optical absorption behavior was investi-
gated by a UV–Visible double beam spectrophotometer (Make:
Cary 5000) using unpolarized light. YVON Florolog-3 (model:
FL3-22) was used to evaluate the photoluminescent characteristics
of prepared nano powders.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Structural studies
Fig. 2 shows the X-ray diffraction spectra of Cu-doped ZnS (0–
4 wt%) nano powders. The spectra revealed three broad peaks at
28.5/C176, 47.6 /C176, and 56.3 /C176. The peak broadening indicates that the
grown powders were nanocrystalline in nature. The observed
peaks were related to the (1 1 1), (2 2 0), and (3 1 1) orientations
of ZnS, as noted in ICDD ﬁle no: 05-0566. Using these crystal
planes, the structure was evaluated to be cubic. Furthermore,
the undoped ZnS power had sharper peaks than the doped ones,
and the peaks became broader as the Cu-doping content was
increased in the powders. This indicates that Cu-doping makes
the powder more nano crystalline. The absence of any other
peaks showed that the prepared powders were free from impurity
phases.

was calculated using Scherrer’s equation, using the (1 1 1) preferred

reported in the literature in dip-coated ZnS with Cu, Al-doping

3.2. Surface morphology studies
Speciﬁc surface area is highly signiﬁcant in adsorption, hetero-
geneous catalysis, and surface reactions [19]. The value of disloca-
tion density was observed to be lower for undoped ZnS nano
powders, which increased with raise in Cu-content in the powder.
The highest value of dislocation density was observed at 4 wt%
copper dopant, representing the greatest hardness among all com-
positions [20]. Similarly, lattice strain and SSA were also increased
with Cu-doping in the powders, which indicate degradation in the
crystalline quality of the powders. Mallika et al. [21] reported the
same results that higher lattice strain caused a reduction in crys-
tallinity and enhanced the peak broadening. Secondly, the high
SSA value is a symptom of a high aspect ratio for nanostructured
materials, resulting in an increased catalytic activity, which was
reported by Sahai et al [22]. The surface morphology of both pure
and ZnS: Cu nano powders was examined using a scanning elec-
tron microscope (SEM), and the related micrographs are given in
Fig. 4. The ﬁgure indicates that ZnS: Cu NPs have a spherical shaped
particle with a random size distribution for 1 wt% and 2 wt% and
changed to ﬂower-like morphology with increase of Cu content
to 3 wt%. Further increase of Cu-doping to 4 wt% resulted in cluster
formation, resembling a bunch of ﬂowers. Compared to pure ZnS
NPs, the particle size was found to be reduced upon Cu-doping.
ZnS: Cu NPs with reduced particle size could be useful for light
trapping in mono-grain solar cells because of multiple reﬂections
of light rays within the surface layer.

properties were measured from 200 nm to 1200 nm wavelength.

Cu2+ ions, which resulted in the appearance of peaks at higher

substituted by copper ions upon doing, the formation of lumines-

demonstrates that Cu 2+ ions successfully substituted Zn 2+ ions in
the ZnS lattice.
4. Conclusions
Pure and ZnS: Cu nano powders were prepared by using chem-
ical co-precipitation technique and physical properties were inves-
tigated with respect to Cu-doping concentration. All the prepared
NPs indicated the (1 1 1) peak as the dominant plane and peak
broadening was noticed upon Cu-doping. This resulted in a
decrease of crystallite size from 7.73 nm to 3.79 nm. A change in
the morphological features was noticed with increase of Cu-
doping in ZnS NPs. The energy gap of ZnS nano powders increased
upon Cu-doping and the photoluminescence data showed the sub-
stitution of Zn 2+ ions by Cu 2+ ions in ZnS lattice. Although increase
of Cu-doping has decreased the crystallinity, however, it enhanced
band gap of the powder. Therefore, such large band gap powders
prepared using a Cu-doping of 4 wt% could be useful as a window
in mono-grain solar cell development.

A B S T R A C T
AgSbS2 has shown promise as an earth-abundant, sustainable light-harvesting material for thin-film solar cells
owing to its suitable optoelectronic properties and high stability. Here, we report the fabrication of AgSbS 2
thin films using a two-stage process (sequential evaporation of Sb/Ag layers and sulfurization at 300–400 ◦C
for 30 min) and their characterization. X-ray diffractometry revealed the formation of Ag 3SbS3 and Sb 2S3
phases, single-phase AgSbS 2, and slight decomposition of AgSbS 2 and the emergence of monoclinic AgSbS 2
at sulfurization temperatures of 300, 350, and 400 ◦C, respectively. The AgSbS 2 films have a cubic crystal
structure with a lattice parameter (a) of 0.565 nm. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed that the
valence states of Ag, Sb, and S were +1, +3, and -2, respectively. Microstructural analysis of the film prepared
at 350 ◦C revealed highly crystalline, large-grains with an average grain size of 5 μm. Optical absorption
studied suggested that the AgSbS 2 film prepared at 350 ◦C exhibited a direct bandgap of 1.61 eV. Hall
measurements revealed an electrical resistivity of 1.52 × 104 𝛺cm, hole mobility of 84.5 cm 2V−1s−1, and a
carrier concentration of 7.95 × 1012 cm−3 for the AgSbS 2 film prepared at 350 ◦C. Finally, AgSbS 2 solar cells
with glass/Mo/AgSbS 2/CdS/indium-tin-oxide/Ag configuration were fabricated (optimal device parameters:
efficiency, 1.1%; open-circuit voltage, 519.6 mV; short-circuit current density, 6.63 mA/cm 2; and fill factor,
31.0%). The device processing conditions must be optimized to further improve the efficiency.
1. Introduction
Thin-film photovoltaics is an emerging area of research with con-
siderable potential. The development of inexpensive and effective pho-
tovoltaic technology is particularly crucial in this regard. Recently,
Cu(In,Ga)Se2 and CdTe-based photovoltaic technologies have recently
achieved optimal levels of development, with their efficiencies exceed-
ing 22% [1]. However, the scarcity and high cost of In and the toxicity
of Cd considerably impede the long-term mass production capability
of these solar cells. Perovskite solar cells have also gained extensive
attention and have achieved efficiencies of over 25% [2] within a span
of 10 years. However, the problems associated with their short lifetime

attractive features such as a direct bandgap close to the optimal value
(1.45 eV) and high optical absorption coefficient ( 𝛼). Among them,
AgSbS2 has emerged as a promising light-harvesting material because
of its non-toxic and earth-abundant elements, as well as its superior
stability. AgSbS2 exhibits a direct bandgap of 1.61–1.75 eV [ 3], high
𝛼 in the visible region, and p-type electrical conductivity. However,
studies on AgSbS2 and its solar cells are quite limited.
Wagner et al. synthesized AgSbS 2 films by a pulsed laser depo-
sition in 2004 [ 4]. Subsequently, Ho and Lee [ 5] prepared AgSbS 2
nanoparticles by heating Ag2S/Sb-S stacks that were deposited on TiO2

prepared cubic AgSbS 2 films by annealing thermally evaporated

tions, which exhibited a photosensitivity of 61%. Zhang et al. [ 8]
fabricated AgSbS2 films via sequential deposition of AgNO 3 and SbCl3
solutions onto TiO 2, followed by sulfurization in a H 2S atmosphere.
Moreover, they fabricated AgSbS 2 semiconductor-sensitized solar cells
with fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO)/TiO2/AgSbS2/Au structure, which
exhibited good photoresponse. Aiswarya et al. [ 9] prepared mon-
oclinic AgSbS 2 by heating CBD-grown Sb 2S3 and thermally evap-
