glass/FTO/n-CdS/p-AgSbS2/C/Ag configuration. The devices exhib-
ited a maximum conversion efficiency of 1.5%, V 𝑂𝐶 of 530 mV,
J𝑆𝐶 of 5.5 mA/cm 2, and FF of 50%. Zhang et al. [ 3] fabricated
AgSbS2 solar cells FTO/TiO2/AgSbS2/Spiro-OMeTAD/Au configuration
using a spin-coating and annealing approach. The solar cells exhib-
ited an optimal efficiency of 2.25%, V 𝑂𝐶 of 433 mV, J 𝑆𝐶 of 10.96
mA/cm2, and FF of 47.50%. Xie et al. [ 10] reported an improve-
ment in the AgSbS 2 solar cell efficiency from 0.27% to 1.30% with
selenization of spray-deposited AgSbS 2 films. They constructed solar
cells in ITO/CdS/AgSbS 2/Au configuration, which exhibited a power
conversion efficiency (PCE) of 1.30%, V 𝑂𝐶 of 420 mV, J 𝑆𝐶 of 8.59
mA/cm2, and FF of 37.0%. Kai et al. [ 11] reported the synthesis of
AgSbS2 thin films and its solar cells by spray pyrolysis method. The
fabricated FTO/compact TiO 2/AgSbS2/spiro-OMeTAD/Au solar cells
exhibited a conversion efficiency of 2.09% with a V𝑂𝐶 of 440 mV, J𝑆𝐶
of 10.49 mA/cm2, and FF of 45.0%.
Despite these efforts to produce AgSbS 2 films and their devices,
highly-crystalline and large-grained films have rarely been fabricated.
A two-stage process involving metallic precursor deposition followed
by sulfurization can permit the growth of highly crystalline and large-
grained AgSbS2 films. The two-stage process is relatively advantageous
among other deposition methods owing to its scalability and high
throughput. CZTS and CTS solar cells fabricated from the two-stage
process exhibited the highest conversion efficiencies [ 12,13]. In the
two-stage process, the precursor layer deposition and sulfurization play
an important role in the growth of high-quality films. In our previous
study, we have used this two-stage process to grow high-quality CuSbS2
films and their solar cells [ 14]. In the present study, we have used
this two-stage process for the growth of AgSbS 2 thin films and their
solar cells. In the first-stage, the Ag and Sb metallic layers were ther-
mally evaporated followed by sulfurization at different temperatures
in the second stage. Highly crystalline single-phase AgSbS 2 films were
consequently obtained, and the AgSbS 2 solar cells constructed in the
substrate configuration exhibited a maximum conversion efficiency of
1.1%.
2. Materials and methods
Ag and Sb slugs (4N purity) that were kept in tungsten boats were
used as the starting materials to prepare the AgSbS 2 films. Prior to the
evaporation, soda-lime glass substrates were soaked in chromic acid
overnight, washed with detergent soap, and ultrasonically cleaned in
acetone, ethanol, and deionized water for 5 min. The cleaned glass
substrates were loaded into a vacuum chamber, which was then set to
a base pressure of 2× 10−6 Torr. The thicknesses of Ag and Sb required
to form 1 μm thick AgSbS 2 were estimated to be 173 and 305 nm,
respectively. The thickness Ag was decreased to 160 nm, whereas Sb
Fig. 1. Schematic of the AgSbS 2 thin film solar cell.
was increased to 320 nm by considering the loss of the low melting
material Sb during sulfurization. Initially, a 320 nm thick Sb layer was
evaporated at 3 Å/s, followed by the evaporation of 160 nm thick Ag
at 3 Å/s onto the substrates. The thicknesses of the metallic stacks were
measured using a quartz crystal thickness monitor. A substrate rotator
was used during the evaporation to uniformly deposit the stacks. No
substrate heating was employed during the evaporation. The sequen-
tially evaporated Sb/Ag metallic stacks were subjected to sulfurization
in a graphite box placed in a quartz tubular furnace to convert them
into AgSbS 2 films. Elemental S powder was used as the source of
sulfur. N2 was filled into the quartz tube to atmospheric pressure for
obtaining a higher sulfur pressure during the sulfurization to suppress
the re-evaporation-induced loss of the elements. The temperature of
the furnace was increased at a rate of 10 ◦C/min up to the desired
temperature (300, 350, or 400 ◦C). The sulfurization was conducted
for 30 min, and the temperature was finally decreased to 250 ◦C at
2 ◦C/min and then left to decrease naturally.
AgSbS2-based thin-film heterojunction solar cells were fabricated in
a substrate configuration with glass/Mo/AgSbS2/CdS/ITO/Ag structure
(as shown in Fig. 1 ) using AgSbS 2 layer (1.2 μm thick) deposited at
300–400 ◦C. A 600 nm thick Mo back contact layer was RF sputtered
at a power of 250 W for 90 min. A 70 nm thick CdS layer was coated
onto the AgSbS 2 absorber via CBD [ 14]. After the CdS deposition, the
AgSbS2/CdS junction was subjected to soft annealing at 100 ◦C for 4 h
on a hot plate to promote stable junction formation. A 300 nm thick
ITO window layer was RF sputtered at a power of 150 W for 60 min
under an Ar pressure of 7.5 × 10−3 Torr. Finally, the Ag front grid
contacts were thermally evaporated to a thickness of 200 nm. Solar
cells (0.36 cm2) were isolated by mechanical scribing for testing.
The crystal structure and phase-purity of the AgSbS 2 films sulfu-
rized at different temperatures were evaluated by acquiring grazing
incidence X-ray diffraction (GIXRD) patterns using a PANalytical X-
ray diffractometer with a Cu K 𝛼 (0.15406 nm) source at an incident
angle (𝜔) of 3◦. The chemical state of the films was evaluated by X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Thermo Scientific, K-Alpha spectrom-
eter) in the range of 0–1200 eV using an Al K 𝛼 source calibrated
to the C 1s line. Prior to the XPS measurements, the samples were
etched for 60 s to remove surface contamination. The morphologies
and thicknesses of the films were accessed by field-emission scanning
electron microscopy (FESEM; Hitachi S-4800). The composition of the
films was determined by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS).

3. Results and discussion
3.1. GIXRD analysis
Fig. 2 shows the XRD patterns of the Sb/Ag stacks sulfurized at
different temperatures. The standard stick patterns of the Ag 3SbS3
(JCPDS Card No. 01-087-0709), cubic AgSbS2 (JCPDS Card No. 01-089-
3669), and monoclinic AgSbS 2 (JCPDS Card No. 019-1137) are also
inserted in Fig. 2 to distinguish AgSbS 2 peaks. The XRD pattern of the
stack sulfurized at 300 ◦C showed dominant and weak diffraction peaks
corresponding to Ag 3SbS3 (JCPDS card no. 01-087-0709) and Sb 2S3
(JCPDS card no. 42-1393), respectively (see * and $ symbols in Fig. 2).
The formation of the secondary Ag 3SbS3 and Sb 2S3 phases indicates
the insufficiency of thermal energy at 300 ◦C for converting the Sb/Ag
stacks into AgSbS2. The XRD pattern of the stacks sulfurized at 350 ◦C
showed diffraction peaks matching the standard stick pattern peaks of
AgSbS2 (JCPDS card no. 01-089-3669), indicating the complete conver-
sion of the Sb/Ag stacks into secondary-phase-free AgSbS 2 within the
XRD probe depth. The films exhibited a cubic crystal structure with a
lattice parameter of 0.565 nm, which is close to the reported lattice
parameter of cubic AgSbS2. The crystallite size of the film, determined
using Scherrer’s formula [15], was found to be 62 nm. The XRD pattern
of the stack sulfurized at 400 ◦C revealed the emergence of monoclinic
AgSbS2 peaks (# symbols in Fig. 2; JCPDS card no. 019-1137) along
with cubic AgSbS 2. An additional peak corresponding to Ag 3SbS3 (*
symbols in Fig. 2) appeared at 400 ◦C owing to slight decomposition
of the AgSbS 2 phase into Ag 3SbS3 and Sb 2S3. The disappearance of
the Sb2S3 peaks could be due to the re-evaporation of the decomposed
Sb2S3 at 400 ◦C. Monoclinic AgSbS 2 has been reported to be a high-
temperature phase, and its presence at this temperature was due to
its polymorphic nature. Based on this investigation, the formation of
AgSbS2 presumably occurred via a solid-state reaction of Ag/Sb during
sulfurization in the following manner: 3Ag + 3Sb + 6S → Ag3SbS3 +
Sb2S3 ⇌ 2AgSbS2. The thicknesses of the films sulfurized at 300, 350
and 400 ◦C were found to be 1.2, 1.2, and 1.1 μm, respectively. We
have estimated the X-ray beam sampling depth using the relation SD
= PD sin𝜔 [16–18], where 𝜔 is the grazing incidence, and PD is the
penetration depth at which the intensity of the X-ray beam reduces to
1/(e) of its initial value. The X-ray sampling depth at𝜔= 3◦ for AgSbS2
was estimated to be 1050 nm.
3.2. Composition
The elemental compositions of the Sb/Ag stacks sulfurized at three
different temperatures are listed in Table 1 . The film sulfurized at
300 ◦C was highly rich in Ag but poor in Sb and S because the low tem-
perature hindered the formation of near-stoichiometric AgSbS 2 films.
In the stacks that were sulfurized at 350 ◦C, the atomic percentages
of Sb and S increased, whereas that of Ag decreased drastically, with
the resulting composition being similar to that of AgSbS 2. A further
increase in the sulfurization temperature to 400 ◦C resulted in the
formation of a slightly Sb-rich films. Overall, the film sulfurized at
350 ◦C showed a near-stoichiometric AgSbS2 composition, considering
the accuracy limits of the EDS analysis (±2 at.%).

3.3. XPS analysis
XPS measurements were performed on the sample prepared at
350 ◦C to determine the chemical states of the films. The survey scan of
the film (Fig. 3a) showed signals due to Ag, Sb, S, and Ar, whereas the
high-resolution Ag3d spectrum ( Fig. 3b) showed two peaks separated
by 6 eV at 373.5 and 367.5 eV, which corresponded to Ag3d 5∕2 and
Ag3d3∕2, respectively. The peak positions and their separation indicate
that the oxidation state of Ag was +1 [9,19]. The high-resolution Sb3d
spectrum (Fig. 3c) showed two intense peaks that were separated by 9.4
eV at 529.3 and 538.6 eV, which corresponded to Sb3d5∕2 and Sb3d3∕2,
respectively. These peak positions and their separation suggest that the
oxidation state of Sb was +3 [ 9,19]. Additionally, two minor peaks
appeared at 536.6 and 527.2 eV, which were assigned to the Sb 𝑜 state
that presumably originated from the Ar+-sputtering-induced reduction,
which is commonly appeared in Sb based compounds [ 9,19,20]. The
narrow S2p scan ( Fig. 3 d) showed two peaks separated by 1.1 eV
at 160.9 and 162.0 eV, which were related to S2p 3∕2 and S2p 1∕2,
respectively; these results indicate that the oxidation state of S was -
2 [9,19]. Therefore, the oxidation states of the elements present in the
films could be expressed as Ag+1Sb+3(S−2)2.
3.4. Morphology
The surface morphologies and cross-sections of the samples sul-
furized at different temperatures were assessed by FESEM ( Fig. 4 ).
The FESEM image of the film sulfurized at 300 ◦C showed two dis-
tinct grains with sizes in the range of 1– 2 μm. The smaller particles
presumably correspond to the Sb 2S3 phase, whereas the larger ones
possibly represent the Ag3SbS3 phase observed in the XRD pattern. The
cross-sectional FESEM image of this film shows the formation of well
adherent film with 1 μmgrains extended vertically up to 1.2 μm. The
micrograph of the film sulfurized at 350 ◦C revealed the formation of
several 6–8 μmsized grains with a compact morphology and 3– 5 μm
sized grains in between them. The cross-section of this film shows the
formation of columnar grains with increased grain size along the thick-
ness (1.2 μm). The crystallization of the large grains at 350 ◦C could
be due to the complete intermixing of the Ag 3SbS3 and Sb2S3 phases
and the formation of single-phase AgSbS 2. The surface morphology of
the film sulfurized at 400 ◦C revealed a decrease in the grain size and
a few cracks on the film surface, which could have been due to slight
re-evaporation of the materials. The cross-sectional image also revealed
the formation of large grains extended along the film thickness. Overall,
the film formed at 350 ◦C exhibited a superior grain growth and a
morphology appropriate for solar cell applications.

3.5. Optical absorption
Spectral transmittance and reflectance curves of the AgSbS 2 films
sulfurized at different temperatures were acquired (Fig. 5a,b). The film
sulfurized at 300 ◦C exhibited 25% transmittance at higher wavelengths
and a continuous decrease in transmittance from 1500 to 750 nm. The
reflectance spectrum of this film exhibit interference fringes and an
onset of absorption at 750 nm. The transition observed at 750 nm might
be due to the dominant Ag 3SbS3 phase present in the film [ 21,22].
The film sulfurized at 350 ◦C showed an enhanced transmittance of
over 50% at higher wavelengths and interference fringes owing to the
crystallization of the compact, large-grained, and single-phase AgSbS 2
films, as indicated by its microstructure. The film exhibited an absorp-
tion onset from 845 to 750 nm, which corresponded to the AgSbS 2
phase. The reflectance spectrum also exhibit interference fringes and
an onset of absorption from 845 nm corresponding to AgSbS 2. The
film sulfurized at 400 ◦C showed diminished interference fringes in
transmittance and reflectance curves and a continuous decrease in
transmittance from 2000 nm owing to the presence of mixed phases
monoclinic and cubic AgSbS2 as well as Ag3SbS3. The onset of absorp-
tion observed at 820 to 720 nm indicates the absorption due to AgSbS2
and Ag3SbS3 phases present in the films.
The Tauc plots were constructed for the films sulfurized at 300–
400 ◦C to determine the optical bandgap (Fig. 6). The direct bandgap of
the film sulfurized at 300 ◦C was found to be 1.75 eV, which is close to
the reported band gap of Ag 3SbS3 [21,22]. The direct optical bandgap
of the film sulfurized at 350 ◦C was estimated to be 1.61 eV, which
is close to the reported bandgap of AgSbS 2 by Zhang et al. [ 3]. The
bandgap of the film sulfurized at 400 ◦C was found to be 1.71 eV. The
increased bandgap of AgSbS 2 at 400 ◦C could be due to the presence
of Ag3SbS3 secondary phase in the film.

density/voltage (J-V) characteristics and cell parameters of the AgSbS2
solar cells are shown in Fig. 7 (a). The solar cell prepared from the

AgSbS2 layer sulfurized at 300 ◦C, exhibited a PCE of 0.6%, J𝑆𝐶 of 4.33
mA/cm2, V𝑂𝐶 of 446.3 mV, and FF of 32.2%. The solar cell fabricated

The solar cell fabricated with the AgSbS 2 layer sulfurized at 400 ◦C,
exhibited a PCE of 0.9%, J 𝑆𝐶 of 6.11 mA/cm 2, V𝑂𝐶 of 519.2 mV,
and FF of 30.0%. The lower device performance of the AgSbS 2 solar
cells fabricated at 300 and 400 ◦C could be due to the formation of
secondary phases in the absorber, whereas the increased efficiency for
the solar cells fabricated at 350 ◦C is attributed to the formation of
phase pure films with high crystallinity and large-grains. The dark J-V
characteristics of the typical solar cell fabricated at 350◦C are shown in
Fig. 7(b) to study the current leakage. The dark J-V curve shows low
current density owing to the improved charge transport and reduced
recombination loss. The cross-sectional FESEM image of the typical
solar cell fabricated at 350 ◦C is also shown in Fig. 7(c) to see the
formation of different layers in the device. The cross-sectional image
of the device confirmed the formation of a compact and large-grained
absorber sandwiched between the compact Mo and CdS/ITO layers.
Notably, the performance of the device reported herein is considerably
inferior to the previously reported highest efficiency of 2.2% for AgSbS2
solar cells [3]. However, the V 𝑂𝐶 of the fabricated device (519.6 mV)
is higher than that reported previously. The lower FF value can be
attributed to the higher series resistance and lower shunt resistance
(Fig. 7a) of the constructed devices. Optimization of the parameters
of each layer during the fabrication is anticipated to provide superior
results, which is the scope of our future work.
4. Conclusions
AgSbS2 films were prepared by sulfurizing thermally evaporated
Sb/Ag metallic precursors at 300–400 ◦C for 30 min. The films sulfur-
ized at 300 ◦C contained the Ag3SbS3 and Sb2S3 phases, whereas those
sulfurized at 350 ◦C contained near-stoichiometric single-phase AgSbS2
with a cubic crystal structure; moreover, the highly crystalline large-
grained films exhibited a direct optical bandgap of 1.61 eV and a hole
mobility of 84.5 cm 2 V−1 s−1. A further increase in the sulfurization
temperature to 400 ◦C led to the emergence of monoclinic AgSbS 2,
dominant cubic AgSbS 2, and an additional Ag 3SbS3 phase. The solar
cells fabricated using the AgSbS 2 absorber layer that was prepared by
sulfurizing the stacks at 350 ◦C exhibited a maximum PCE of 1.1%,
V𝑂𝐶 of 519.6 mV, J 𝑆𝐶 of 6.63 mA/cm 2, and FF of 31.0%. Further
optimization of the processes and clarification of the properties of each
layer are imperative for achieving superior device performance.

Effect of KNN substitution on the structural, 
electrical, and piezo characteristics of lead‑free 
0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO3 ceramics
Nalamala Srinivasa Rao1, B. Srikanth1, T. Anjaneyulu2, P . Mohan Babu3, M. Bhaskaraiah4, 
K. N. V. Lakshmi5, and Kuppam Mohan Babu6,*

ABSTRACT
The conventional solid-state reaction approach was employed to develop 
0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3 and 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3–KNN lead free electro ceramics. 
Both ceramics coexist in the rhombohedral structural phase (R3c) and tetragonal 
structural phase (P 4mm) regions. When  K0.5Na0.5NbO3 (KNN) is introduced to 
0.94Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3–0.06SrTiO3, the structure grows more symmetric without com-
promising electrical polarization. The surface morphology of both ceramics is 
measured by the average grain size, which is reduced somewhat from 3 to 2.6 μm, 
resulting in the influence of KNN. The composition-induced local structural tran-
sition—i.e., the change from order to disorder-occurs when KNN is added to the 
0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO3 binary system. Additionally, the depolarization temperature 
(Td) increases substantially with the inclusion of KNN. When KNN is present, the 
coercive field (E c) dramatically reduces from 32 to 21 kV/cm (~ ΔE = 11 kV/cm), 
without impairing the remaining remnant polarization (P r). When compared to 
0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO3, the substitution of KNN produces a high strain response of 
roughly 0.25% (under a mild field of 60 kV/cm). The longitudinal strain value of 
140pC/N was determined parallelly. As a result, both of these lead-free ceramics 
are attractive prospects for next-generation electro ceramic applications.

SrTiO3 (ST) has a perovskite structure with cubic 
symmetry at room temperature. Previous studies 
showed that ST replacement of BNT was an effective 
technique for modifying the dielectric, piezoelectric, 
and ferroelectric features. At a critical composition of 
0.28, Hiruma et al. found an important electric-field 
produced strain response [25–27]. However, the study 
focused mainly with room temperature. To encour -

on enhancing the required properties by introduces 
KNN into 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO3. The primary goal was 
to establish a correlation between the structural and 
electrical features of these specimens.
2  Experimentalprocedure
To create the eco-friendly (1 − x) 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO3–x 
KNN ( x = 0 & 0.01) ceramics, the usual solid-state 
approach was used. The raw oxide materials (AR-
grade) and carbonate were combined in a stoic pro-
portion based on their weight percentage. These 
powdered oxides and carbonates were ball milled in 
ethyl alcohol for 10 h at 300 rpm. These dried pow-
ders were calcined at 800 °C for 3 h, milled for 10 h at 
300 rpm, and mixed with 4 wt% polyvinyl alcohols 
for dry powders before being formed into a circular 
1 Introduction
Materials having many window operations are 
more appealing for today’s generation of applica-
tion. Because of their numerous features, including 
structural, electrical, and optical ones (when an f-shell 
element is present), ferroelectric materials represent a 
distinct class [1 –4]. Due to a lack of efficiency, per-
formance, and inadequate improvement of those 
required features, the current generation application 
still has an open window for the new material system. 
Ferroelectric systems are better ideal for improving 
such features by substituting them with alternative 
cations of appropriate sizes [5–7]. For modern applica-
tions such actuators & energy storage, materials hav-
ing morphotropic phase boundaries (MPB) are more 
appealing. Due to both structural phases’ collective 
additive qualities, which are the current emphasis 
at MPB, the desirable attributes are enhanced [8 –10]. 
In light of this, PZT and its derivatives excel for the 
required commercial need [11– 13]. The primary 
worry is regarding lead (Pb), which is very poison-
ous and harmful in nature and has significant health 
concerns, even though Pb-based materials offer out-
standing ferro/piezoelectric characteristics for device 
applications. The European Union’s Restriction of 
Hazardous Substances (ROHs) Directive committee 
has started to limit hazardous substances including 
Pb-based electrical and electronic components [14, 
15]. There is an open window to replace these lead 
contained materials to replace the leaf free materi-
als. Sodium bismuth titanate  Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3 (NBT) is 
one attractive contender because to its strong room 
temperature ferro electricity and good piezoelectric 
characteristics [16, 17]. MPB solid solutions based on 
BNT, such as  Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3–BaTiO 3 (NBT–BT) and 
 N a0.5Bi0.5TiO3–Bi0.5K0.5TiO3 (NBT–BKT), were devised 
and produced to reduce electrical conductivity while 
also improving electromechanical responses [18, 19].
Despite significant developments and the demon-
stration of a few ultrasonic devices with acceptable 
performance, the overall piezoelectric capabilities of 
the lead-free substitutes were still inferior to the lead-
based system. The issue of how to improve piezoelec-
tric response is not only scientifically fascinating, but 
also technologically essential for piezoelectric device 
applications. Kounga and Zhang et al. have reported 
an extensive electric-field-induced strain response 
in  Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3–K0.5Na0.5NbO3 (BNT–KNN) and

A field emission scanning electron microscope was

3  Resultsanddiscussion
The structural data (X-ray diffraction) of lead-free 
0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3 and 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3–KNN 
ceramics is shown in Fig. 1. These patterns show that 
both are crystallized into pure perovskite structures 
without secondary phases coexisting. The morpho-
logical structures from 20 to 80° demonstrate that 
there are no superlattice reflections caused by the 
oxygen octahedral tilt. Figure 1 shows the enhance 
portion of the (111) PC pseudocubic representation 
to confirm the effect/substitution of KNN over the 
0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3. The displacement of the Bragg 
peak towards the lower angle side of the (111)PC peak 
indicates diffusion of KNN into 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3. 
These ceramics structural existence is compared with 
duel phase model, which is found to be in good 
agreement with the duel phase rhombohedral struc-
tural phase (R 3c) and tetragonal structural phase 
(P4mm) regions. The polarities will be moved parallel 
to the A-site and B-site cations, as well as the direc-
tions of the (111) Bragg peaks, because the rhombo-
hedral structure is non-centrosymmetric and polar 
in order [28]. As a result, the addition of KNN will 
cause the long-range polar phase to be interrupted. 
Rietveld refinement was used to confirm the struc -
tural phase contribution/quantitative phase fractions 
over the substitution of KNN in 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3 
structural refinement of the XRD measurement. Sev-
eral dual phase models, including rhombohedral 
(R3c) and tetragonal (P 4mm), provide a reasonable 
match with stable fitting parameters. When com-
pared to the P4mm space group, R3c makes a sig-
nificant contribution. Table 1 shows the improved 
parameters for understanding the quality of fit. The 
refinement graph, as well as the Braggs locations and 
pseudocubic representations, are illustrated in Fig. 2.  
The surface morphology of 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3 
and 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3–KNN is shown in Fig. 3. 
Both surfaces are pore free according to this surface 
morphology. Each grain is easily identifiable by its 
distinctive grain boundaries and homogeneous grain 
distribution throughout all morphological micro-
structures. There was no evidence of phase segrega-
tion at the grain boundaries. In the presence of KNN, 
a little fluctuation in grain size throughout the whole 
surface indicated the compounds even distribution. 
The line intercept method (ASTM International) can 
be used to assess the grain size distribution of these 
specimens [29]. The Gaussian distribution func-
tion was used to optimize the average grain size, 
as illustrated in Fig. 2. For 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3 and 
0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3–KNN, the average grain size is 
found to be 3 μm and 2.6 μm, respectively (Fig. 4).

The temperature-dependent dielectric constant

obey the Curie–Weiss formula at this phase transi-
tion. The diffusiveness coefficient γ decides whether

calculated γ values are found to be quite comparable,

in compared to 0.94NBT–0.06SrTiO 3 lead to a more 
diffusive dielectric response. Figure 5 depicts the 
acquired results.

ABSTRACT
The structural ambiguity was resolved quantitatively with dual-phase models 
of Cc + P4mm. Multiple-phase transition behaviors including Antiferroelectric 
(AFE) to Ferroelectric transition, transition at depolarization temperature, and 
AFE to paraelectric state transition were observed among PLZST samples and 
investigated in detail. The piezoelectric and impedance features of a modified 
PZT ceramic that has different mole ratios of La and Sn co-substitution are shown 
here. The principle of Archimedes shows that the synthesized specimens have 
sufficient density for withstanding high temperatures and higher fields while 
explaining them. We concentrated on the impedance and piezoelectric coefficients 
 d33,   g33, and figure of merit (FOM) of the ideal  PbLaZrSnTiO3 (PLZST) composi-
tion (50/30/20) in this study. The PLZSTs consist of two phases (Cc + P4mm), which 
combine to generate a single phase with a high Sn content and a low La content. 
These structural correlations coexist with the dual evaluation of impedance and 
piezoelectric characteristics in order to produce optimum composition. In order to 
evaluate the impedance features, the property of activation energy for the grains 
also supports the PLZST (50/30/20) having superior properties among PLZSTs. 
The optimum composition will meet the current business’s commercial needs 
through multiple windows.

1 Introduction
Multifunctional materials or ceramics have attracted 
a lot attention in the modern era due to their numer-
ous window operations [1–3]. PZT and its analogs are 
widely used in the communication, medical, and elec-
trical industries due to their low cost and outstanding 
accuracy. PZT’s outstanding characteristics have appli-
cations in energy storage devices as well as positive 
and negative electro-caloric properties [4 , 5]. Because 
of their remarkable properties, multiple organizations 
[6–9] have looked into the PZT and PLZT systems 
simultaneously; as a consequence, these materials are 
opening new avenues to address current generation 
concerns [10–12]. They showed, for instance that these 
materials are outstanding for electro-caloric effect 
cooling because of their significant dipolar entropy 
shift during the transition from the antiferroelectric 
to the ferroelectric phase. These ceramic specimens 
involve crystallite grains of different sizes that are 
linked together in a variety of arbitrarily ways [9, 13]. 
These zones of grain amalgamation are referred to as 
boundaries of grain, and they are greatly impacted by 
external factors such as heating and cooling, an exter-
nal electric field, and so on. The interfacial behavior 
of grain boundaries enables electroceramics [ 8, 14]. 
In device application, all ceramic specimens are con-
nected to the system through electrodes. These elec-
trodes can function as a grain-to-grain barrier system 
with programmable effect settings [15]. Impedance 
spectroscopy is an invaluable tool to determine the 
entire profile picture of the grain and grain bound-
ary profile. The results of impedance spectroscopy 
not only provide values for grain contribution and 
grain boundary, but also provide a comparable cir-
cuit model for modeling [ 16, 17]. Even if the model 
has been taken into account, choosing one that works 
might be hard. A particular model was developed for 
these PLZST specimens to draw the proper predicted 
outcomes and provide information for the design of 
advanced devices. The fault makeup of solid-state 
specimens plays an important role in these new poten-
tial applications. Understanding how desired charac-
teristics interact with imperfections and vacancies on 
the site was important [18, 19]. The co-substitution of 
La and Sn in varying ratios affects interior imperfec-
tions such as voids at A- and B-sites. Site vacancies 
and electrons at space charges affect the ferroelectric 
fatigue or impedance/conductive properties of mate-
rials [20– 23]. The use of AC impedance analysis for 
identifying the cause of failure at grain–grain bounda-
ries is an adaptable technique. It must also build its 
relaxation method by providing distinctive resistance 
and capacitance values to the grain and grain border 
effects.
The excellent properties of PZT have drawn a lot of 
attention in the area of polar-based materials devices. 
The pure form of PZT has a higher  d33 value when 
compared to all polar materials [24]. The increased 
value of  d33 in PZT produced by altering the phase 
boundary additionally indicates an important increase 
in device effectiveness. Piezo-coefficients have been 
produced in this instance by averaging many internal 
ionic crystal polarizations. These piezo-coefficient val-
ues are a consequence of stationary charges building 
up at both ends caused by crystal structural deforma-
tion. This domain mobility has discovered applica-
tions in power-controlling electric devices [25]. These 
devices have controls, and their efficiency/perfor-
mance is evaluated using a figure of merit (FOM).
2  Experimentaldetails
The PZT-based polycrystalline ceramics  (Pb0.94La0.06)
(ZrxSn0.30Ti0.70−x)O3(x = 0.54, 0.52, 0.50, and 0.48) have 
been synthesized using a conventional solid-state reac-
tion. The high-grade raw metal oxide chemical pow-
ders of PbO,  La2O3,  TiO2,  ZrO2, and  SnO2 (99% AR 
Grade, Chemicals) were used as initial precursors for 
synthesis. These raw materials were weighed accord-
ing to their mole ratio and mixed properly. The mixed 
powders were further mixed properly using ball mill-
ing over the time 10 h with 300 rpm for all specimens 
and then calcined at 840 °C for 3 h. After mixing uni-
formly, these powders were pressed into circular 
disks with a uniform thickness of 10 mm diameters 
by adding 8 wt% of PVA (Poly vinyl Alcohol) as binder 
solution prepared in IPA solution. These circular 
disks were sintered in alumina crucibles in the pres-
ence of PZT powder to play down the lead volatiliza-
tion and then placed in a box furnace. These circular 
disks were sintered at 1250 °C for 3 h with a uniaxial 
rate of heating of 5 °C/min. These ceramics were pol-
ished on different emery sheets for a fine thickness of 
0.2 mm with a uniform surface. The structural phase 
purity of polycrystalline ceramics was confirmed by 
using X-ray diffractometer (XRD, 7000S/L, Shimadzu 
Corp, Japan) using Cu Kα radiation. The temperature-
dependent dielectric and impedance measurements on

the disk with electrodes were performed by using a 
computer-controlled LCR meter (Tonghui TH2828S, 
China) within the temperature range from − 5 to 600 °C 
with a uniform heating rate of 2 °C/min. The speci-
mens were poled electrically at room temperature in a 
silicon oil bath (DOW CORNING 704) by applying DC 
electric fields of 0–60 kV/cm for constant time for each 
equal interval of time. These piezocoefficients were 
estimated with the help of Piezometer System PM300 
(Piezotest Ltd.) operated at a frequency of 100 Hz.
3  Resultsanddiscussion
An efficient method for determining the structural 
distortion of polycrystalline materials is the X-ray 
diffraction (XRD) technique. Figure 1 shows the XRD 
patterns of Zr- and Ti-substituted PZT (PLZST) ceram-
ics. Every ceramic was stabilized in a pure perovskite 
structure, devoid of any secondary phases coexisting 
with it. Super lattice reflections of monoclinic Cc have 
been described in literature paired with the room-
temperature structure, specifically for PZT [26]. As 
Zr content increases at the Ti site, the peak combines 
and appears as a single peak. The existence of dual 
phase over the substitution of Zr- and Ti-substituted 
PZT, analyzed phase contribution quantitatively 
employing a methodical structural refinement proce-
dure. Throughout the series, Rietveld refinement was 
performed using full proof software [27]. We choose 
various dual structural phase models to erform refine-
ment by validating the structural coexistence. In order 
to determine the coexistence of the structural phase 
model for PLZST (50/30/20),  the clear indication is 
yielded that fit was extremely good fit with Cc + P4mm. 
The quality and goodness of fit for PLZST (50/30/20) 
are shown in the inset of Fig. 1.The inset shows the evi-
dence of the significant intense Brag reflection of the 
(110)pc peak’s best fit. The refine parameters, atomic 
positions, and lattice constants are provided in Table 1.
The temperature-dependent dielectric permittivity 
(ε) and tangent loss (tan δ) of the unpoled samples 
under a selected frequency of 100 kHz are presented 
in Fig. 2.The dielectric anomaly indicated by  Tm, which 
is the most significant dielectric constant value and 
is related to the phase transition from the antiferro-
electric to the paraelectric region, was seen in each 
specimen. For each specimen, the phase transition 
sequence exhibits a comparable pattern. At the lower 
temperature side (before depolarization T d), the permit-
tivity decreases with compositional variation and all 
exhibit broad peaks, suggesting the features of a dif -

4  Conclusions
A solid-state approach was employed to successfully 
produce high-density pure phase polycrystalline 
materials. The structural phase purity of these sub-
stances was quantified via structural refinement. From 
structural phase purity, it was confirmed that PLZST 
ceramics were successfully synthesized via a solid-
state route. The dual phase presence of P4mm and 
Cc over the co-substitution of  Zr4+and  Ti4+ in PLZST 
(50/30/20) ceramics confirms the contribution of both 
polarization directions. The piezoelectric and imped-
ance studies suggested that the PLZST (50/30/20) is 
the most effective composition. The estimated activa-
tion energy of these specimens also supports the ideal 
composition. This perfect chemical is a viable choice 
for meeting the commercial needs of industries.
